items.stem: The Plaza Accord of September 1985 was an agreement among five major economies to do what?
options: Halt the fall of the US dollar and stabilise exchange rates around current levels
Launch the European Monetary System
Restore the convertibility of the dollar into gold
Drive down the US dollar, especially against the yen and the Deutsche Mark

steps: In September 1985, at the Plaza Hotel in New York, the G5 countries (US, Japan, West Germany, France and the UK) agreed on coordinated intervention to depreciate a very strong dollar.
Over the following two years the dollar lost about half its value against the yen.
In February 1987 the Louvre Accord sought instead to halt the decline and stabilise exchange rates.
explanation.shortcut: First push, then brake: the Plaza (1985) pushes the dollar down, the Louvre (1987) stops its fall.
explanation.trap: Stabilising the dollar after its fall is the aim of the Louvre Accord, two years later. The EMS (1979) is a purely European arrangement.
explanation.rule: The exchange rate is an economic policy lever, and coordinated interventions work when they are consistent with interest rates. For an exporter, the exchange rate can move margins more than an efficiency programme.

items.stem: On 'Black Monday', 19 October 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by roughly how much in a single day?
options: About 12%
About 8%
About 23%
About 40%

steps: On 19 October 1987 the Dow lost 22.6% in a single session, the worst one-day percentage fall in its history.
Portfolio insurance helped to amplify the crash: automatic strategies that sold index futures as prices fell, fuelling further selling.
After the crash, circuit breakers were introduced, automatic trading halts in the event of extreme falls; the Fed provided liquidity to the system.
explanation.shortcut: In 1987 the market wiped out more than a fifth of its value in a day: 'more than 20%' is the order of magnitude to remember.
explanation.trap: About 12% is the fall on dramatic days such as 28 October 1929 or 16 March 2020: huge, but about half of 1987.
explanation.rule: Strategies that sell when prices fall create feedback loops: the same mechanism was seen with LDI funds in 2022. Liquidity disappears exactly when it is needed.

items.stem: On 'Black Wednesday', 16 September 1992, which currency was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM)?
options: The French franc
The Deutsche Mark
The British pound
The Spanish peseta

steps: The UK raised its official rate from 10% to 12% and announced a further rise to 15%, but sterling kept falling and that evening it left the ERM.
The underlying cause: after reunification the Bundesbank kept rates high, and the countries pegged to the Deutsche Mark had to follow it despite their weaker economies.
A well-known hedge fund made about $1 billion betting against sterling; the next day Italy also suspended the lira from the exchange rate arrangements.
explanation.shortcut: Black Wednesday is British history: sterling leaves, the French franc holds, the peseta is devalued but stays in.
explanation.trap: The peseta was devalued in the same crisis but did not leave the ERM; the franc came under attack in 1993 and was saved by widening the fluctuation bands to 15%.
explanation.rule: A fixed exchange rate with diverging fundamentals and free capital movement offers speculators an asymmetric bet: this is also why the euro was created as a single currency rather than as a peg.

items.stem: The Nasdaq Composite peaked in March 2000. Roughly how much did it fall from that peak to its low in October 2002?
options: About 78%
About 35%
About 50%
About 95%

steps: The Nasdaq closed at about 5,048 points on 10 March 2000 and hit about 1,114 on 9 October 2002: a fall of about 78%.
Many listed companies had no earnings and were valued on metrics such as users or 'eyeballs'; when markets stopped funding them, many went bust.
The index climbed back above its 2000 high only in 2015, fifteen years later.
explanation.shortcut: From over 5,000 to just over 1,000: you have lost almost four-fifths.
explanation.trap: About 50% is the fall in the S&P 500 over the same period: the Nasdaq, concentrated in technology, fell much further.
explanation.rule: A high multiple prices in future growth: if growth disappoints, de-rating and falling earnings arrive together. In any valuation, always ask what growth is already in the price.

items.stem: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008. As of 2025, which statement about that filing is correct?
options: It was the first failure of a US bank since the 1930s
It was resolved over a weekend through a government-backed sale to a rival
It was the first bankruptcy ever filed under Chapter 11
It was the largest bankruptcy filing in US history by assets

steps: Lehman had about $640 billion of assets: its Chapter 11 filing remains the largest bankruptcy in US history.
In March 2008 Bear Stearns had been sold in a hurry to a competitor, backed by Fed financing; no buyer was found for Lehman and the state did not step in.
The failure froze the interbank and commercial paper markets; the next day the Fed had to rescue AIG, and TARP followed in October.
explanation.shortcut: Bear Stearns (March) = rescued through a sale; Lehman (September) = allowed to fail. Hence the debate on who is 'too big to fail'.
explanation.trap: The rushed weekend sale with public support describes Bear Stearns, not Lehman. And bank failures in the US were nothing new: hundreds failed in the 1980s.
explanation.rule: Very short-term funding (repo) for a highly leveraged intermediary can vanish within days: liquidity, not only solvency, decides survival.

items.stem: The 'Big Bang' of 27 October 1986 in the City of London refers to:
options: The privatisation of the Bank of England, which had been state-owned since 1946
The abolition of UK exchange controls, letting capital move freely in and out of Britain
The creation of a single regulator for all UK banks, insurers and investment firms
Stock Exchange deregulation: fixed commissions ended and outside owners allowed in

steps: Big Bang abolished fixed commissions, ended the separation between jobbers (market makers) and brokers, and allowed outside firms, including foreign ones, to buy stock exchange member firms.
Trading left the exchange floor and moved to banks' dealing rooms: on-screen prices (the SEAQ system) and orders by telephone.
Large American and European banks bought up the British brokers: this is the origin of the City as a global investment banking hub.
explanation.shortcut: Big Bang = an explosion of competition: negotiable commissions, open ownership, screens instead of the floor.
explanation.trap: The Bank of England was not privatised: it had been nationalised in 1946 and gained operational independence over interest rates in 1997. The single regulator arrived only between 1997 and 2001, while exchange controls had already been abolished in 1979.
explanation.rule: Competition on commissions and foreign capital explain why so many investment banks have their European base in London, and why the City also competes on regulation.

items.stem: The South Sea Bubble burst in Britain in 1720. Which scheme, devised by John Law, collapsed in France in the same year?
options: The Dutch East India Company
The Banque de France note issue
The Mississippi Company scheme
The Suez Canal Company

steps: In 1716 John Law founded the Banque Générale (the Banque Royale from 1718), which issued banknotes, and in 1717 the Mississippi Company, later merged into the Compagnie des Indes.
The scheme swapped French public debt for shares in the company, while the bank printed money that financed the purchase of those same shares: the price soared and then collapsed in 1720.
In England the South Sea Company carried out a similar conversion of public debt into shares, with the same outcome.
explanation.shortcut: 1720 is the year of the twin bubbles: South Sea in London, Mississippi in Paris, both based on converting public debt into shares.
explanation.trap: The Banque de France was founded only in 1800 and the Suez Canal Company in 1858. The VOC was Dutch and dates from more than a century earlier.
explanation.rule: When money creation finances the purchase of assets, asset prices run ahead of the real economy: a useful lesson whenever abundant liquidity and valuations are discussed.

items.stem: After peaking in September 1929, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89% by 1932. Roughly when did it regain its 1929 nominal peak?

steps: From its peak of about 381 points (September 1929) the Dow fell to about 41 in July 1932, a drop of 89%.
To get back to 381 from 41 the value has to multiply more than 9 times: the nominal peak was surpassed only in November 1954, 25 years later.
Taking into account reinvested dividends and the deflation of the 1930s, the real recovery was much faster, but the nominal figure remains the symbol of how long the damage lasted.
explanation.shortcut: After an 89% fall, 11% of the value remains: getting back to the starting point takes about +800% (1 / 0.11 = 9 times).
explanation.trap: 1936 is tempting because the market rose a great deal from 1932, but starting from 41 points the Dow peaked at around 190 in 1937, roughly half the 1929 high.
explanation.rule: Losses and gains are asymmetric: -50% requires +100%, -89% requires about +800%. That is why controlling drawdowns matters as much as average return.

items.stem: Which US law repealed the Glass-Steagall provisions that kept commercial banks and securities firms under separate ownership?
options: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002
The Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking Act of 1994
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999

steps: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (1999) repealed the rules that prohibited affiliations between commercial banks and securities firms, allowing groups that combine banking, investment banking and insurance.
The law followed the 1998 merger that created Citigroup by combining a large bank with an insurance and financial group, a deal that without reform would have required divestments.
Riegle-Neal (1994) had liberalised interstate branching, Sarbanes-Oxley (2002) concerns governance after the accounting scandals, and Dodd-Frank (2010) is the post-crisis reform.
explanation.shortcut: Match laws and dates: 1933 separates (Glass-Steagall), 1999 reunites (Gramm-Leach-Bliley), 2002 governance (Sarbanes-Oxley), 2010 post-crisis reform (Dodd-Frank).
explanation.trap: Dodd-Frank goes in the opposite direction: through the Volcker Rule it restricts banks' proprietary trading, reintroducing a partial separation.
explanation.rule: The universal bank model that dominates today stems from this repeal: understanding it helps you read organisation charts and potential conflicts between corporate banking and investment banking.

items.stem: What was the core of the 'Nixon shock' of August 1971?
options: A devaluation of the dollar against European currencies within the European Monetary System
The suspension of the dollar's convertibility into gold for foreign central banks
The creation of the IMF's Special Drawing Rights
A US embargo on oil imports from OPEC countries

steps: On 15 August 1971 the US president closed the 'gold window': foreign central banks could no longer convert dollars into gold at 35 dollars an ounce.
The package also included an additional 10% tariff on imports and a temporary freeze on prices and wages.
After the attempted rescue through the Smithsonian Agreement (December 1971), the main currencies began to float from 1973.
explanation.shortcut: August 1971 = end of the dollar-gold link, i.e. the end of Bretton Woods. From then on money is purely fiduciary (fiat).
explanation.trap: Special Drawing Rights have existed since 1969, and the EMS is a European system dating from 1979 in which the dollar was not involved.
explanation.rule: Since 1971 the value of money has depended on the credibility of the central bank, not on a physical reserve: this is the basis for understanding inflation, exchange rates and the role of gold as a reserve asset.

items.stem: In October 1979 the Federal Reserve, led by Paul Volcker, changed its approach to fight double-digit inflation. What did it do?
options: It announced a formal 2% inflation target to anchor expectations
It targeted bank reserves and money growth, letting interest rates rise as high as needed
It pegged the dollar to the Deutsche Mark to import the Bundesbank's anti-inflation credibility
It capped 10-year Treasury yields through large-scale bond purchases

steps: On 6 October 1979 the Fed moved from directly controlling interest rates to controlling the growth of bank reserves and money, accepting much higher and more volatile rates.
The fed funds rate approached 20% in 1981; CPI inflation, about 14.8% in March 1980, fell below 4% in 1983.
The cost was a double-dip recession (1980 and 1981-82), with unemployment close to 11%.
explanation.shortcut: Volcker = very high rates to break inflation expectations, accepting a recession.
explanation.trap: The formal 2% inflation target is much more recent: the Fed only announced it explicitly in 2012.
explanation.rule: A central bank's credibility is built by accepting short-term costs: the Volcker reference resurfaced everywhere in 2022 and explains the logic of 'higher for longer'.

items.stem: The 1997 Asian financial crisis began when Thailand floated the baht. Which balance-sheet weakness made it so damaging for local banks and companies?
options: Long-term fixed-rate borrowing in local currency, mostly held by domestic pension funds and insurers
Short-term borrowing in US dollars used to fund long-term assets earning local-currency revenues
Large holdings of US Treasuries that lost value when US rates rose
Equity ratios so high that firms could not raise new bank credit

steps: On 2 July 1997 Thailand floated the baht after burning through its reserves to defend the peg to the dollar; the crisis spread to Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Banks and companies had borrowed short term in dollars to finance property and investment with revenues in local currency: a double mismatch, of currency and of maturity.
With the devaluation, dollar debt exploded in local-currency terms and foreign creditors stopped rolling over their loans; IMF programmes with heavy conditions followed.
explanation.shortcut: Hard-currency debt + local-currency revenues + short maturities = a devaluation turns into a solvency crisis.
explanation.trap: Long-term debt in local currency is precisely the structure that protects a country: it is what emerging economies have tried to build since 1997.
explanation.rule: In the credit analysis of an emerging-market issuer, always look at the share of unhedged hard-currency debt and at short-term maturities: that is where crises start.

items.stem: In July 2012 the ECB President pledged to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro. Which instrument was announced soon afterwards to back that pledge?
options: The Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP)
The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI)
Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT)
Targeted Longer-Term Refinancing Operations (TLTRO)

steps: On 26 July 2012, in London, the then ECB President Mario Draghi said the ECB would do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.
In September 2012 the ECB announced OMT: potentially unlimited purchases of short-term government bonds (1 to 3 years) of countries under an adjustment programme with the bailout fund (ESM).
The instrument was not activated in the following years: the announcement alone was enough to drastically reduce Italian and Spanish spreads.
explanation.shortcut: Order by crisis: 2012 sovereign debt = OMT, 2014 weak credit = TLTRO, 2020 pandemic = PEPP, 2022 rate hikes = TPI.
explanation.trap: TPI is the modern cousin of OMT, but it was created in July 2022, during the rate-hiking cycle, with different access criteria and without an ESM programme.
explanation.rule: A credible central bank can calm a market without spending: the promise of a backstop reduces redenomination risk and therefore the spread.

items.stem: The Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), enacted in October 2008, authorised the US Treasury to use up to how much?
options: USD 85 billion
USD 700 billion
USD 250 billion
USD 2 trillion

steps: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of October 2008 authorised the Treasury to use up to 700 billion dollars.
Created to buy 'toxic' assets, TARP was used mainly to inject capital into banks (Capital Purchase Program, up to 250 billion), as well as for AIG and the auto sector.
85 billion, by contrast, was the Fed's initial loan to AIG, in September 2008.
explanation.shortcut: The signature number of the crisis is 700: huge, but still in billions, not trillions.
explanation.trap: 250 billion is the portion earmarked for direct recapitalisation of banks, i.e. part of TARP, not the total authorised.
explanation.rule: Recapitalising with equity is faster and more effective than buying illiquid assets at uncertain prices: it is the logic behind almost all subsequent bank rescues.

items.stem: In February-March 2020, the S&P 500 fell into a bear market (down more than 20% from its high). What was distinctive about that episode?
options: It was the fastest fall of that size on record, and the index regained its high by August 2020
It lasted more than three years before the index recovered
It was triggered by the failure of a large European bank
It happened while the Federal Reserve was raising interest rates aggressively to fight inflation

steps: From its high on 19 February 2020 the S&P 500 entered a bear market in about 16 trading sessions and hit its low on 23 March, a fall of about 34%.
The Fed cut rates to zero on 15 March and on 23 March announced asset purchases with no predetermined limits; huge fiscal stimulus followed.
The index returned to its highs in August 2020: the fastest bear market and one of the quickest recoveries in history.
explanation.shortcut: Pandemic = everything very fast: a crash in weeks, a policy response in days, a recovery in months.
explanation.trap: A multi-year recovery describes 2000-02 and 2008-09, not 2020: the difference was the speed and size of the response by the Fed and governments.
explanation.rule: Market reactions depend on the policy response as much as on the shock: that is why analysts follow central banks and fiscal policy as closely as fundamentals.

items.stem: On 20 April 2020, the expiring front-month WTI crude oil futures contract settled at about minus USD 37 per barrel. What was the main reason?
options: OPEC countries agreed to pay buyers to take surplus oil off the market
An exchange software error that produced prices which were later cancelled
US sanctions temporarily banned the physical delivery of crude oil
Storage at the delivery hub was nearly full, so holders paid to avoid delivery

steps: The WTI future involves physical delivery at Cushing, Oklahoma. With demand collapsing because of the lockdowns, storage tanks were almost full.
Anyone holding the expiring contract who could not take delivery of the crude had to close the position at any price: on 20 April the settlement price was about -37.6 dollars.
Contracts with later expiries stayed positive: the market was in extreme contango.
explanation.shortcut: Negative price = paying someone to take away something you cannot keep. If you have nowhere to store the oil, the oil becomes a cost.
explanation.trap: The price was real and was not cancelled: it was not a technical error but a physical logistics and storage problem.
explanation.rule: Physically delivered futures reflect logistics at expiry, and anyone rolling futures in contango loses value: the spot price is not the return the investor earns.

items.stem: During the 2022 inflation surge, euro area annual HICP inflation peaked at roughly what level, and when?
options: About 10.6% in October 2022
About 7.4% in March 2022
About 14.6% in December 2022
About 9.1% in June 2022

steps: Euro area inflation reached 10.6% year on year in October 2022 (in March it was 7.4% and still rising), driven above all by energy after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and by the post-pandemic reopening.
The ECB raised rates for the first time in eleven years in July 2022 and took the deposit rate from -0.50% up to 4% by September 2023.
In the United States CPI inflation had peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, four months before the euro area: the energy shock hit Europe for longer.
explanation.shortcut: Remember 'double digits': in 2022 euro area inflation exceeded 10%, the highest since the euro was created.
explanation.trap: The 9.1% of June 2022 is the peak of US CPI inflation, not the euro area's. 14.6% is too high for the area average: similar or higher values were seen only in some individual countries, such as the Baltic states.
explanation.rule: The move from negative rates to 4% changed the cost of capital: lower multiples, more expensive LBOs and more attention to duration risk on the balance sheets of banks and insurers.

items.stem: Which combination of factors best explains the US regional bank failures of spring 2023?
options: Losses on subprime mortgage-backed securities and complex CDOs
Unrealised losses on long-dated bonds plus flighty uninsured deposits
Defaults on large loans to emerging-market governments
Trading losses hidden in off-balance-sheet investment vehicles and derivatives

steps: In 2020-21 some regional banks gathered large amounts of deposits and invested them in long-dated Treasuries and MBS with low yields.
With the 2022 rate hikes the value of those securities collapsed; for securities classified as held-to-maturity the losses did not go through the income statement, but they were real.
Many deposits exceeded the insured limit of 250,000 dollars: when depositors realised this, withdrawals, including via apps, were extremely fast and some banks failed within days.
explanation.shortcut: 2008 = poor-quality assets (subprime). 2023 = good-quality assets but with too much duration, funded by unstable deposits.
explanation.trap: Subprime and CDOs are the 2008 crisis: in 2023 the problem was not credit risk but interest-rate and liquidity risk.
explanation.rule: When analysing a bank, look at unrealised losses on the securities portfolio and the composition of deposits: ALM risk can bring a bank down even without non-performing loans.

items.stem: Which sequence best describes Japan's experience in the years after the 1985 Plaza Accord?
options: Yen depreciation, an export boom, then a decade of double-digit inflation
Yen appreciation, monetary easing, then an asset bubble that burst around 1990
A banking crisis in 1986, then a fixed peg of the yen to the US dollar
An immediate recession, then the adoption of a currency board to stabilise the yen

steps: After the Plaza Accord the yen appreciated strongly ('endaka'); to support the economy the Bank of Japan cut the discount rate to 2.5% in 1987.
Easy credit and optimism inflated equities and property: the Nikkei ended 1989 close to 38,900 points.
Monetary tightening in 1989-90 burst the bubble; years of deflation and banks full of bad loans followed (the 'lost decade'). The Nikkei surpassed its 1989 peak only in February 2024.
explanation.shortcut: Strong currency, low rates to compensate, bubble, burst: the sequence starts from a strong yen, not a weak one.
explanation.trap: Yen depreciation with an export boom is the opposite of what the Plaza Accord set out to achieve: the aim was precisely to strengthen the yen against the dollar.
explanation.rule: A debt-financed property bubble leaves behind a long 'balance sheet recession': companies and banks pay down debt instead of investing, and low rates alone are not enough.

items.stem: The hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management nearly collapsed in 1998. Which statement best describes its losses and how the crisis was resolved?
options: Unhedged short positions in technology stocks lost money in the dot-com rally, and the US Treasury bailed the fund out with public money
Leveraged convergence trades failed after Russia's default; private banks recapitalised it in a New York Fed-brokered rescue
Losses on subprime mortgages forced its nationalisation by the Federal Reserve
A rogue trader hid losses on Japanese stock index futures for years, and the fund was sold to a foreign bank for a nominal price

steps: LTCM, founded in 1994 and with two Nobel laureates among its partners, ran convergence trades: it bought relatively cheap securities and sold similar, more expensive ones, betting that the spread would close, with leverage of about 25 times capital.
After Russia's default in August 1998 investors rushed into the most liquid and safest securities: spreads widened instead of closing, on almost all positions at the same time.
In September 1998 the New York Fed brought together 14 financial institutions, which put in about 3.6 billion dollars to take over the fund and wind it down in an orderly way, with no public money.
explanation.shortcut: LTCM = leverage + convergence bets + flight to liquidity. The rescue was private, coordinated by the public sector.
explanation.trap: The rogue trader hiding losses on Japanese futures and the sale for a nominal sum describe the collapse of Barings in 1995, a different case.
explanation.rule: In a crisis correlations tend to 1 and liquidity disappears: diversified but leveraged positions can all lose together. Systemic risk can also arise from a highly interconnected private fund.

items.stem: The Greek private sector involvement (PSI) of March 2012 is best described as:
options: The largest sovereign restructuring in history at the time, with a nominal haircut of about 53.5%
A buyback of Greek bonds at par, financed entirely by an IMF loan
A unilateral default declared without any agreement with creditors
A restructuring of official loans only, leaving all privately held bonds untouched and fully paid

steps: In March 2012 private holders of about 200 billion euros of Greek bonds exchanged them for new bonds, accepting a 53.5% cut in face value; the loss in present-value terms was estimated at between about 60% and 75%.
Greece retroactively inserted collective action clauses (CACs) into its Greek-law bonds, binding dissenting creditors as well; ISDA declared a credit event and the CDS paid out.
The PSI was part of the second European and IMF aid programme and was the first debt restructuring by a euro area country.
explanation.shortcut: Remember two facts: 'just over half of face value' and 'the largest ever'. They are enough to frame it.
explanation.trap: A unilateral default without agreement describes cases such as Argentina in 2001: Greece instead negotiated an exchange, reinforced by the CACs.
explanation.rule: The law governing a bond matters: local-law bonds can be amended by the national legislature, foreign-law bonds (for example English law) only with the majorities set out in their clauses. It is a key factor in pricing sovereign risk.

items.stem: In March 2023, after several US regional banks failed, the Federal Reserve created the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP). What was its key feature?
options: One-year loans against high-quality securities valued at par, not at market value
Direct purchases of bank shares to recapitalise weak lenders
A permanent guarantee of all deposits at every US bank, whatever the size of the account
New unlimited dollar swap lines with all foreign central banks

steps: The BTFP lent for up to one year against Treasuries, agency securities and MBS, valuing them at par rather than at market price, which after the rate hikes was much lower.
This let a bank obtain liquidity without selling the securities and crystallising the unrealised losses, breaking the spiral of withdrawals, forced sales and losses.
In parallel, for the failed banks the authorities used the systemic risk exception to protect uninsured deposits as well; the programme stopped making new loans in March 2024.
explanation.shortcut: The problem was good securities trading below par: the solution was to lend against them as if they were worth par.
explanation.trap: There was no blanket guarantee of all deposits in the system: cover above 250,000 dollars applied to depositors at the failed banks and was decided case by case.
explanation.rule: Distinguish liquidity from solvency: a solvent bank can fail because of a bank run, and the lender of last resort exists precisely to prevent that.

items.stem: In late September 2022, the Bank of England launched temporary purchases of long-dated gilts. What was the main source of the market stress it was addressing?
options: A failed auction of index-linked gilts caused by a computer outage at the debt office
A run on retail deposits at several large UK high-street banks
Sterling's forced exit from a currency peg against the euro after a speculative attack
Pension funds' leveraged LDI hedges faced collateral calls as long gilt yields jumped

steps: After the announcement, on 23 September 2022, of unfunded tax cuts, long-dated gilt yields rose by more than a percentage point within a few days, to above 5% on the 30-year.

Many defined benefit pension funds hedged their liabilities with leveraged LDI strategies (swaps and repo): the rise in yields triggered collateral calls that forced them to sell gilts, pushing yields even higher.
On 28 September the Bank of England announced temporary purchases of long-dated gilts to break the spiral, ending them in mid-October.
explanation.shortcut: 'Safe' hedges + leverage + margin calls = forced selling. It is the dynamic of 1987, but in the bond market.
explanation.trap: Sterling's forced exit from an exchange-rate regime is 1992 (Black Wednesday): in 2022 sterling fell, but there was no peg to defend.
explanation.rule: Fiscal credibility is priced into yields within days, and the leverage hidden in hedging strategies can turn into systemic liquidity risk.

items.stem: In 1925 Britain returned to the gold standard at the pre-war parity. Why is this widely seen as a policy mistake?
options: Sterling was undervalued at that parity, causing an export boom and high inflation
Sterling was overvalued, forcing deflation and unemployment until Britain left gold in 1931
It tied sterling to the US dollar rather than to gold, importing US monetary policy directly
It required Britain to run large budget deficits to buy enough gold reserves

steps: In 1925 the United Kingdom restored gold convertibility at the pre-war parity (about 4.86 dollars per pound), even though wartime inflation had eroded British competitiveness.
With an overvalued pound, adjustment had to come through falling wages and prices: high unemployment, weak exports and social tension, culminating in the General Strike of 1926.
Keynes criticised the decision as early as 1925; in September 1931 Britain abandoned gold and sterling devalued.
explanation.shortcut: Pre-war parity after years of inflation = an exchange rate that is too strong. Going back to the old price when the world has changed means overvaluation.
explanation.trap: Undervaluation and inflation are the opposite of what happened: the British mistake was deflationary. The hyperinflation of the 1920s is a German case (1923).
explanation.rule: An overvalued fixed exchange rate is paid for with domestic deflation: it is the same dilemma faced by the peripheral euro countries in 2010-12, which could not devalue.

items.stem: On which date was the euro introduced as the currency of 11 EU countries, initially for non-cash transactions only?
options: 1 January 2002
1 November 1993
1 January 1999
1 January 1993

steps: From 1 January 1999 the euro became the currency of 11 countries, Italy included: the ECB began running the single monetary policy and exchange rates were irrevocably fixed.
For three years the euro existed only as book money (accounts, transfers, securities); banknotes and coins arrived on 1 January 2002.
The Maastricht Treaty entered into force on 1 November 1993, while the single market started on 1 January 1993.
explanation.shortcut: 1999 = euro on the markets and in accounts, 2002 = euro in your wallet.
explanation.trap: 2002 is the date everyone remembers because it is when the banknotes arrived, but government bonds and markets had been in euros since 1999.
explanation.rule: In historical data series the monetary watershed is 1999, not 2002: Italian interest rates and market prices have been in euros since then.

items.stem: At what irrevocably fixed rate were Italian lire converted into euros?
options: 1,936.27 lire per euro
1,000 lire per euro
1,955.83 lire per euro
2,000 lire per euro

steps: The conversion rate was fixed on 31 December 1998: 1 euro = 1,936.27 lire, to six significant figures, effective from 1 January 1999.
The other rates were fixed in the same way: for example 1 euro = 1.95583 German marks.
In everyday life people used the approximation '1 euro is about 2,000 lire', which however should never be used in calculations.
explanation.shortcut: Remember 1936: almost 2,000, but not quite. Mental maths: divide the lire by 2,000, then add about 3%.
explanation.trap: 1,955.83 is a false friend built on the Deutsche Mark rate (1.95583 marks per euro): similar digits, different currency.
explanation.rule: Conversion rates are fixed and are not rounded: historical accounts, prices and debt in lire are always converted by dividing by 1,936.27.

items.stem: Which pair of fiscal reference values was set in the framework of the Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992?
options: Government deficit of 3% of GDP and government debt of 60% of GDP
Government deficit of 3% of GDP and government debt of 90% of GDP
Government deficit of 1% of GDP and government debt of 60% of GDP
Government deficit of 0.5% of GDP and government debt of 100% of GDP

steps: The Maastricht Treaty, signed in February 1992 and in force from November 1993, set out the path to monetary union and the convergence criteria.
The fiscal parameters are a government deficit of no more than 3% of GDP and government debt of no more than 60% of GDP.
The debt criterion allowed a higher ratio if it was 'sufficiently diminishing': that is why Italy joined the euro in 1999 with debt well above 100% of GDP.
explanation.shortcut: The two numbers are linked: with nominal growth of 5%, a steady 3% deficit brings debt to 60% of GDP in the long run (3 / 5 = 60%).
explanation.trap: The 90% comes from a well-known and much-debated academic study on debt and growth, not from the Treaty. The 0.5% is the structural deficit limit in the 2012 Fiscal Compact.
explanation.rule: 3% and 60% remain the reference points even after the 2024 reform of EU economic governance: markets read every Italian budget against these numbers.

items.stem: Italy was one of the six founding members of the European Economic Community. Which treaty created it in 1957?
options: The Treaty of Paris
The Maastricht Treaty
The Treaty of Rome
The Treaty of Lisbon

steps: The Treaties of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957, established the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom.
The six founders were Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
The Treaty of Paris (1951) had created the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC); Lisbon (2007) is the latest major reform of the treaties.
explanation.shortcut: Common market = Rome 1957; coal and steel = Paris 1951; single currency = Maastricht 1992; institutional reform = Lisbon 2007.
explanation.trap: The Treaty of Paris came earlier and covered only coal and steel: the EEC, with its customs union, was born in Rome.
explanation.rule: European integration started with trade and arrived at money: that is why EU powers over competition and the internal market are strong, while its fiscal powers are much weaker.

items.stem: The EU single market is built on the 'four freedoms'. Which list is correct?
options: Free movement of goods, services, capital and data
Free movement of goods, services, capital and persons
Free movement of goods, energy, capital and persons
Free movement of goods, services, currency and pensions

steps: The single market guarantees the free movement of goods, services, capital and persons between member states.
It was formally completed on 1 January 1993, on the basis of the 1986 Single European Act and a programme of about 300 legislative measures.
The four freedoms do not, however, remove tools such as foreign investment screening (FDI screening) or merger control.
explanation.shortcut: Think about what moves: things (goods), work done for others (services), money (capital), people. Four, no more.
explanation.trap: In the European debate there is sometimes talk of a 'fifth freedom' (knowledge, research or data), but the treaties provide for only four: data is not one of them.
explanation.rule: In a cross-border deal within the EU, freedom of establishment and of capital is the rule, but golden power, antitrust and sector rules remain the real conditions precedent.

items.stem: What best describes an Italian 'industrial district' (distretto industriale)?
options: A special economic zone offering tax breaks and fast-track permits to investors
An area dominated by a single large state-owned plant and its local suppliers
A free-trade zone around a major port, exempt from customs duties
Many specialised SMEs in one sector and its supply chain, clustered in one area

steps: A district is a defined area in which many SMEs in the same sector and its supply chain work side by side: they specialise in individual stages, compete and collaborate.
Economists speak of 'Marshallian' external economies: skilled labour, specialised suppliers and knowledge that circulates within the area.
Classic examples: tiles in Sassuolo, eyewear in the Belluno area, textiles in Prato, sports footwear in Montebelluna.
explanation.shortcut: District = many small firms, one trade, one territory.
explanation.trap: Special economic zones (ZES) also exist in Italy, but they are a policy tool with tax and administrative incentives, not a spontaneous phenomenon of local specialisation.
explanation.rule: Many Italian mid-market targets are district champions: understanding the local supply chain helps you assess real market share, power over suppliers and buy-and-build opportunities.

items.stem: In September 1992, during the European currency crisis, what happened to the Italian lira?
options: It left the Exchange Rate Mechanism and depreciated sharply
It was replaced by the euro at a fixed conversion rate
Its ERM band was widened to 15%, which kept it inside the mechanism
It joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism for the first time, at a fixed central rate

steps: On 17 September 1992, one day after sterling, Italy suspended the lira from the EMS exchange-rate arrangements and the lira devalued sharply.

That year the government passed a very tough budget package, including an extraordinary levy of 6 per thousand on bank deposits (July 1992), and the agreement with the social partners definitively did away with the scala mobile wage indexation.
The lira rejoined the EMS in November 1996, a necessary step to join the euro in 1999.
explanation.shortcut: September 1992: sterling and the lira leave the EMS together. The lira rejoins in 1996, just in time for the euro.
explanation.trap: The lira was not joining the EMS for the first time: it had been part of it since 1979, left in 1992 and rejoined in 1996. The widening of the bands to 15% came only in August 1993 and helped the currencies that remained in the system, such as the French franc.
explanation.rule: 1992 is the turning point for Italian public finances: privatisations, primary surpluses and convergence towards Maastricht all stem from that crisis.

items.stem: In Italian financial news, 'lo spread' usually refers to:
options: The gap between the ECB deposit facility rate and its main refinancing operations rate
The difference between Italian and euro area inflation
The bid-ask spread on FTSE MIB index futures
The yield difference between 10-year Italian BTPs and 10-year German Bunds

steps: The spread is the yield difference between the 10-year BTP and the 10-year German Bund, expressed in basis points (100 basis points = 1 percentage point).
The Bund is considered the least risky bond in the euro area: the spread measures the premium demanded for Italy risk (credit, liquidity and, in crises, redenomination risk).
Example: a BTP at 3.8% and a Bund at 2.5% give a spread of 130 basis points.
explanation.shortcut: Spread = BTP minus Bund, both 10-year, in basis points.
explanation.trap: The corridor between the ECB's rates is something else: it concerns monetary policy, not Italian sovereign risk.
explanation.rule: The spread feeds into the cost of capital of Italian banks and companies: when it rises, so do the cost of debt and the reference rate used in valuing Italian assets.

items.stem: What is a BTP (Buono del Tesoro Poliennale)?
options: A zero-coupon Italian Treasury bill with a maturity of up to 12 months, issued at a discount
A floating-rate Italian government note indexed to Euribor
A bond issued by the Bank of Italy to drain liquidity from banks
A fixed-coupon Italian government bond, medium to long term, with semi-annual coupons

steps: The BTP is the Italian medium to long-term government bond with a fixed coupon paid every six months: it is the main source of financing for the public debt.
The BOT, by contrast, is short term (up to 12 months) and has no coupon: you buy it below par and receive 100 at maturity. The CCTeu is floating rate, indexed to 6-month Euribor.
There are also inflation-linked BTPs: the BTP Italia (Italian inflation) and the BTP€i (euro area inflation).
explanation.shortcut: BOT = short, no coupon. BTP = multi-year, fixed coupon. CCT = floating coupon.
explanation.trap: The zero-coupon bill of up to 12 months is the BOT: the acronyms look alike but describe instruments that are opposite in maturity and structure.
explanation.rule: The 10-year BTP is the benchmark for Italy risk: its yield is the reference for pricing Italian corporate and bank bonds.

items.stem: In 2021, Borsa Italiana, the Milan stock exchange, was acquired by which exchange group?
options: London Stock Exchange Group
Deutsche Börse
Euronext
SIX Group

steps: The Milan Stock Exchange was founded in 1808, in the Napoleonic era; after its privatisation in the 1990s, it merged with the London Stock Exchange in 2007.
In 2021 Borsa Italiana joined the Euronext group, which also runs, among others, the Paris, Amsterdam and Brussels exchanges.
The main index is the FTSE MIB, made up of 40 stocks and historically heavily weighted towards banks, energy and utilities.
explanation.shortcut: First London (2007-2021), then Euronext: today Milan is part of a network of continental exchanges.
explanation.trap: London Stock Exchange Group really was the owner from 2007 to 2021, which is why it is the most tempting answer: but in 2021 it was the seller, not the buyer.
explanation.rule: The FTSE MIB, weighted towards banks and utilities, often behaves like a bet on spreads and rates: bear this in mind when comparing multiples and performance with other European indices.

items.stem: How was Next Generation EU, the recovery instrument agreed in 2020, mainly financed?
options: By the ECB creating money and transferring it to member states
By a new EU-wide corporate income tax
By the European Stability Mechanism lending out its existing paid-in capital to governments
By the European Commission borrowing on capital markets on behalf of the EU

steps: Next Generation EU is worth about 750 billion euros at 2018 prices (about 800 at current prices) and is financed by bond issuance by the Commission on behalf of the EU, including green bonds.
It is the first time the EU has borrowed jointly on this scale; the loans must be repaid by 2058.
The ECB cannot finance states directly: the prohibition of monetary financing is written into the treaties (Article 123 TFEU).
explanation.shortcut: NGEU = common European debt: the Commission issues on behalf of the EU, and the EU budget repays by 2058.
explanation.trap: The ECB buys bonds on the secondary market for monetary policy purposes, but it cannot transfer money to states: that option is prohibited by the treaties.
explanation.rule: With NGEU the EU has become one of the large supranational issuers in euros, a quasi common 'safe asset' that sits alongside Bunds, OATs and BTPs on the yield curve.

items.stem: Under the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility, what makes Italy's national plan (PNRR) stand out among member states?
options: Italy is the largest recipient in absolute terms, combining grants and loans
Italy received only grants and requested no loans
Italy is the only country whose plan is financed directly by the ECB rather than the EU
Italy's plan has the smallest allocation relative to GDP

steps: Italy's PNRR was worth about 191.5 billion euros in its original version (about 69 in grants and 123 in loans), rising to about 194 billion with the 2023 revision that incorporated REPowerEU.

It is the largest plan in absolute terms among EU countries, ahead of Spain's. After the revisions, however, Spain receives more in grants: Italy's lead comes from its large share of loans. On top of this there is a national complementary fund of about 30 billion.

The resources are organised into missions (digitalisation, green transition, infrastructure, education and research, inclusion, health) and at least 40% of those that can be allocated by territory goes to the Mezzogiorno.
explanation.shortcut: Italy = largest plan, because it requested both the grants and a very high share of loans.
explanation.trap: Several large countries, such as France and Germany, requested only grants: Italy instead also made massive use of the loans, and that is what makes it the largest recipient.
explanation.rule: The PNRR has been the engine of Italian public investment until 2026: for construction, infrastructure and digital, the end of the funds is a risk to factor into projections.

items.stem: Under the Maastricht convergence criteria, a candidate's inflation rate must be no more than 1.5 percentage points above the average of:
options: The three best-performing member states in price stability
The euro area as a whole, weighted by GDP
Germany alone, as the anchor currency country
The European Central Bank's 2% target for consumer price inflation

steps: The inflation criterion compares the candidate country with the average of the three member states with the lowest inflation (the best performers in price stability): the maximum margin is 1.5 percentage points.
The long-term interest rate criterion uses the same three countries with a margin of 2 points; on top of these come deficit, debt and at least two years in ERM II without severe tensions.
There is also legal convergence: the national central bank must be independent and its statute compatible with that of the European system.
explanation.shortcut: 1.5 for inflation, 2 for rates, 2 years in ERM II, and always 'the best three' as the yardstick.
explanation.trap: Germany was the de facto reference in the 1990s, but the criterion is formally tied to the three best-performing countries, which can change from one assessment to the next.
explanation.rule: The convergence criteria explain how a country joins the euro: it must show that it has imported monetary credibility before giving up its own currency.

items.stem: As of 2025, which countries take part in the EU single market through the European Economic Area (EEA) without being EU members?
options: Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein
Switzerland, Norway and Iceland
The United Kingdom, Norway and Switzerland
Turkey, Norway and Iceland

steps: The European Economic Area, in force since 1994, extends the single market to Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, which adopt most EU rules without voting on them.
Switzerland is a member of EFTA but rejected EEA membership in a 1992 referendum: its relations with the EU are based on bilateral agreements.
Turkey has a customs union with the EU for industrial goods, which does not include the free movement of persons and services.
explanation.shortcut: EEA = the three small countries of the North and the Alps: Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein. Switzerland is a case of its own.
explanation.trap: Switzerland is the most tempting choice because it is in EFTA and highly integrated with the EU, but it is not in the EEA.
explanation.rule: There are several models of integration with the EU (member, EEA, bilateral agreements, customs union): telling them apart helps you understand market access and the passporting of financial services.

items.stem: Which pairing of an Italian industrial district and its specialisation is correct?
options: Prato: ceramic tiles
Sassuolo: woollen textiles
Belluno area: eyewear
Valenza: sports footwear

steps: The eyewear district is concentrated in the Belluno area (Cadore and Agordino), in Veneto, and is one of the world's leading hubs for the sector.
The other correct pairings are: Sassuolo for ceramic tiles, Prato for woollen textiles, Valenza for jewellery, Montebelluna for sports footwear.
Each district concentrates skills, suppliers and brands in the same territory, often with many family businesses.
explanation.shortcut: Glasses in the mountains (Belluno), tiles in Emilia (Sassuolo), wool in Tuscany (Prato), jewellery in Piedmont (Valenza).
explanation.trap: All the wrong options pair a real district with another district's specialisation: it is the classic 'right name, wrong product' distractor.
explanation.rule: Knowing Italy's industrial geography makes a pitch credible: knowing where a sector's competitors, suppliers and talent are located supports a consolidation thesis.

items.stem: Compared with Germany and France, Italy's business sector is best characterised by:
options: A higher share of employment in large firms with more than 250 employees
More jobs in micro and small firms, and a smaller average firm size
A dominant role of state-owned groups in manufacturing since the 2000s
A much lower weight of manufacturing in value added than France

steps: In Italy the share of employment in micro-enterprises (fewer than 10 employees) is much higher than in Germany and France, and average firm size is among the lowest in Europe.
At the same time Italy has one of the largest manufacturing sectors in Europe: the weight of manufacturing in value added is higher than in France.
The business landscape is dominated by family firms; mid-sized exporters (the so-called 'fourth capitalism') are the most dynamic segment.
explanation.shortcut: Italy = many small family firms, but strong manufacturing. Do not confuse 'small' with 'not very industrial'.
explanation.trap: Those who associate 'small firms' with 'little industry' choose the option about manufacturing weighing less than in France: it is false, the opposite is true.
explanation.rule: Small size, family ownership and generational handovers are the engine of mid-market M&A and private equity in Italy: they are the backdrop to many mandates.

items.stem: The '4A' of 'Made in Italy', named after the Italian words for four sectors, refers to:
options: Food, fashion, furniture and home, automation and machinery
Automotive, aerospace, agriculture and armaments manufacturing
Food, fashion, furniture and home, automotive and car design
Banking, insurance, asset management and accounting services

steps: The 4As are Alimentare (food), Abbigliamento-moda (clothing and fashion), Arredo-casa (furniture and home) and Automazione-meccanica (automation and machinery): the sectors in which Italy has its greatest competitive advantages in exports.

Mechanical engineering, i.e. machinery and industrial automation, carries more weight than people think: in foreign trade statistics machinery has for years been one of the top items in Italian exports.
The model combines quality, market niches and district supply chains, rather than large volumes or low prices.
explanation.shortcut: The four As are Italian words: Alimentare (eating), Abbigliamento (dressing), Arredo (living at home), Automazione (making machines).
explanation.trap: Two traps: English words starting with A (automotive, aerospace, agriculture, armaments), whereas the acronym comes from Italian; and cars in place of automation. The fourth A is capital-goods engineering, not the motor car.
explanation.rule: When you analyse an Italian company, link it to the supply chain in which it excels: foreign buyers and funds are looking for exactly these competitive advantages.

items.stem: The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno, active from 1950 to 1984, was created to:
options: Manage the conversion of the lira into the euro
Rescue Italian banks and industrial groups after the 1929 crisis
Finance infrastructure and industrial development in Southern Italy
Administer Marshall Plan funds on behalf of all Western European recipients

steps: The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno was set up in 1950 to finance land reclamation, aqueducts, roads and later large industrial plants in Southern Italy.

In the first decades the gap with the North narrowed, but over time inefficiencies emerged and the large industrial hubs ('cathedrals in the desert') failed to create a widespread productive fabric; it was abolished in 1984.
The North-South gap remains structural: the PNRR requires at least 40% of the resources that can be allocated by territory to go to the Mezzogiorno.
explanation.shortcut: Mezzogiorno in the name = Southern Italy. 1950 = post-war period and reconstruction.
explanation.trap: Rescuing banks and industrial companies after the 1929 crisis was the task of IRI, founded in 1933: another large public body, with a different mission.
explanation.rule: The territorial gap affects productivity, the labour market and credit risk: in analyses of Italian companies or banks, geographic exposure matters.

items.stem: What was Italy's IRI (Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale), founded in 1933?
options: A public agency set up to supervise Italian banks and protect savers after the 1929 crash
The regulator of the Milan stock exchange until the creation of Consob
A national cooperative bank created to finance agricultural producers
A state holding that took over banks' industrial stakes, wound up after privatisations

steps: IRI was created in 1933 to rescue the large mixed banks, which were loaded with industrial stakes after the 1929 crisis: the State took over those stakes and control of the banks.
After the war it became one of Europe's largest state-owned holding companies, active in steel, telecommunications, motorways, shipbuilding and banking.
In the 1990s, with the privatisations linked to fiscal consolidation and Maastricht, it was turned into a joint-stock company, dismantled and put into liquidation in 2000.
explanation.shortcut: IRI = the State as entrepreneur: born from a bank rescue (1933), ended with the privatisations (1990s).
explanation.trap: Banking supervision was reorganised by the 1936 Banking Law and later entrusted to the Bank of Italy, while the stock exchange is supervised by Consob, created in 1974: IRI was an owner of companies, not an authority.
explanation.rule: Many large listed Italian groups stem from the IRI and privatisation era: this explains the still significant presence of the State as shareholder and its special powers.

items.stem: In November 2011, at the peak of Italy's sovereign debt stress, the 10-year BTP-Bund spread reached roughly:
options: About 150 basis points, with 10-year BTP yields near 3%
About 1,500 basis points, with 10-year BTP yields above 15%
About 250 basis points, with 10-year BTP yields near 4%
Above 500 basis points, with 10-year BTP yields above 7%

steps: In summer 2011 the Greek crisis spread to Italy and Spain; in November the BTP-Bund spread rose above 500 basis points (peaking at around 575) and the 10-year BTP yield went above 7%.
7% was seen as a critical threshold: similar levels had preceded the bailout requests of Greece, Ireland and Portugal.

In November the government changed and in December came the 'Salva Italia' decree, with a large fiscal package and a pension reform; however, the spread only fell durably after the 'whatever it takes' of July 2012.
explanation.shortcut: Remember '7 and 500': yield above 7%, spread above 500 basis points.
explanation.trap: 1,500 basis points are Greek levels, not Italian ones: Greece's spread went well beyond these values, Italy's did not.
explanation.rule: With debt above 100% of GDP, every extra point of yield weighs on the public finances as the debt is rolled over: that is why the spread is a political as well as a financial variable.

items.stem: Bund yields are unchanged while the 10-year BTP-Bund spread widens from 150 to 250 basis points. With a modified duration of about 8, roughly what happens to the price of an existing 10-year BTP?
options: It falls by about 1%
It is unchanged because the coupon is fixed
It rises by about 8%
It falls by about 8%

steps: If the Bund does not move, a 100 basis point rise in the spread equals a 1 percentage point rise in the BTP yield.
Approximate price change = - modified duration × change in yield = -8 × 1% = about -8%.
A bank holding 10 billion of BTPs with a similar duration would lose about 800 million in market value.
explanation.shortcut: Price and yield move in opposite directions and duration is the multiplier: 100 basis points times a duration of 8 gives 8%.
explanation.trap: The -1% confuses the change in yield (1 point) with the change in price: without multiplying by duration you underestimate the loss eightfold.
explanation.rule: This is why the spread and Italian banks move together: the banks hold large amounts of domestic government bonds, and sovereign stress becomes stress on their capital.

items.stem: On Borsa Italiana's main market (Euronext Milan), the STAR segment is designed for:
options: Small companies listing under lighter rules on a multilateral trading facility
Mid-caps that accept stricter transparency, liquidity and governance requirements
The largest blue-chip companies, those included in the FTSE MIB index
Exchange-traded funds, certificates and other exchange-traded products

steps: STAR stands for Segmento Titoli con Alti Requisiti, the high-requirements securities segment (today Euronext STAR Milan): it is the segment of the main market for mid-sized companies that accept stricter obligations on disclosure, liquidity (with a specialist) and governance.
In return they gain greater visibility with institutional investors, especially foreign ones.
Small companies with lighter requirements list instead on Euronext Growth Milan (formerly AIM Italia), a multilateral trading facility.
explanation.shortcut: STAR = 'Alti Requisiti' (high requirements): the name says it all. Mid-sized companies that commit to more, not less.
explanation.trap: The market with light requirements for SMEs is Euronext Growth Milan: confusing the two segments is the most common mistake.
explanation.rule: For an Italian mid-sized company the choice of listing segment determines costs, obligations and investor base: it is one of the first questions in an ECM mandate.

items.stem: Under the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the core of Next Generation EU, how were funds paid to member states?
options: In instalments, each conditional on meeting agreed milestones and targets
As a single upfront transfer proportional to population
Only as reimbursement of invoices already paid, as with the EU's traditional cohesion funds
Automatically each year, based on each country's GDP growth

steps: The RRF is a performance-based instrument: after initial pre-financing of 13%, each instalment is paid only if the country shows it has reached the agreed milestones and targets.
The milestones cover both investments and reforms, for example in justice, public administration and competition.
The regulation set 31 August 2026 as the deadline for completing milestones and targets and 31 December 2026 as the deadline for payments.
explanation.shortcut: RRF = payment by results: no milestones, no instalment.
explanation.trap: Reimbursement of expenses already incurred is the model of traditional cohesion funds: the RRF pays against results, not against invoices.
explanation.rule: Execution risk (the capacity to spend and implement) is the real issue with the PNRR: it affects growth, public procurement and sectors such as construction and infrastructure.

items.stem: Italy's 'golden power' rules allow the government to:
options: Set the offer price in initial public offerings of companies considered strategic
Nationalise any company with more than 250 employees without paying compensation
Veto or set conditions on deals in strategic sectors such as defence and energy
Override ECB supervisory decisions on significant banks based in Italy

steps: The golden power was introduced in 2012 and replaced the old 'golden share', which had been judged incompatible with EU law.

The government can veto, impose conditions on or oppose the acquisition of stakes in strategic sectors: defence and national security, energy, transport, communications and, after successive extensions, also finance, health and agri-food.
Relevant transactions must be notified to the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, which has set deadlines to decide.
explanation.shortcut: Golden power = the government's screen on investment in strategic sectors. It does not set prices and does not nationalise.
explanation.trap: Supervision of significant banks lies with the ECB and the government cannot override it: the golden power assesses the national interest, not prudential stability.
explanation.rule: In an M&A deal in Italy the golden power notification is often a condition precedent: it must go into the timetable and the deal documents from the outset.

items.stem: The 1979 'Cassis de Dijon' ruling of the European Court of Justice established which principle central to the single market?
options: The primacy of Community law over any conflicting national law
Mutual recognition: goods lawfully sold in one member state can in principle be sold in all
Taxation of VAT in the country of destination of the goods
The general prohibition of state aid that favours national champion companies over rivals

steps: Germany banned the sale of the French liqueur Cassis de Dijon because its alcohol content was below the German minimum for fruit liqueurs.
The Court ruled that a product lawfully marketed in one Member State must, in principle, be admitted in the others, unless mandatory requirements such as health or consumer protection apply.
Mutual recognition avoided the need to harmonise every single technical standard and made the single market programme of the 1980s possible.
explanation.shortcut: Cassis = a liqueur trying to cross a border: the ruling is about the movement of goods, hence mutual recognition.
explanation.trap: The primacy of Community law was established in 1964 by the Costa v ENEL judgment, which arose from an Italian case on the nationalisation of electricity.
explanation.rule: A similar logic underpins the European 'passport' in financial services: an authorisation obtained in one country opens access to the others.

items.stem: What did the 1981 'divorce' between the Bank of Italy and the Italian Treasury change?
options: The Treasury stopped issuing bonds denominated in lire
The Bank of Italy lost the power to issue banknotes
Italian government debt was transferred to the European Monetary Institute for management
The Bank of Italy no longer had to buy government bonds left unsold at auctions

steps: Until 1981 the Bank of Italy had to buy the government bonds left unsold at auctions: in effect it financed the deficit by creating money.
With the 'divorce' (a letter from the Treasury Minister to the Governor in February 1981, effective from July) that obligation ended and the Treasury had to fund itself in the market at market rates.
Inflation fell over the 1980s, but higher real rates and large deficits caused the debt-to-GDP ratio to rise rapidly.
explanation.shortcut: Divorce = the central bank stops being the buyer of last resort of Treasury bonds.
explanation.trap: The European Monetary Institute was only created in 1994, as the forerunner of the ECB: in 1981 it did not exist and no debt was ever transferred to it.
explanation.rule: The ban on monetary financing is now written into the EU Treaties: that is why the spread genuinely reflects fiscal sustainability and cannot be 'cancelled' by printing money.

items.stem: In August 2011, as Italian and Spanish bond yields surged, how did the ECB respond?
options: It launched Outright Monetary Transactions, conditional on an ESM programme
It started the Public Sector Purchase Programme, its first large-scale QE
It extended its Securities Markets Programme (SMP) purchases to Italy and Spain
It cut its deposit rate below zero for the first time in its history

steps: The Securities Markets Programme was launched in May 2010 for Greece; in August 2011 the ECB also started buying Italian and Spanish bonds.
At the same time the ECB sent the Italian government a letter requesting reforms and fiscal consolidation: central bank support was in effect tied to economic policy commitments.
SMP purchases were limited and sterilised: they were not enough, and the spread peaked in November 2011.
explanation.shortcut: Put the tools in order: SMP 2010-12, OMT 2012, negative rates 2014, QE (PSPP) 2015, PEPP 2020, TPI 2022.
explanation.trap: OMT was the 2012 response, after 'whatever it takes': in 2011 the ECB was still using the more limited SMP.
explanation.rule: Central bank support for sovereign bonds always comes with conditions: it is a key element in assessing Italy risk even today.

items.stem: In July 2022 the ECB created the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI). What was its stated purpose?
options: To counter unwarranted, disorderly spread moves that block policy transmission
To finance the green transition through direct ECB loans to non-financial firms
To provide cheap long-term funding to banks that increase their lending
To guarantee bank deposits across the euro area up to a common limit per depositor

steps: The TPI was announced on 21 July 2022, together with the ECB's first rate hike in eleven years, to prevent the hike from causing unwarranted widening of some countries' spreads.
It allows secondary market purchases of the bonds of a country whose financing conditions deteriorate without justification in the fundamentals.

Access depends on criteria: compliance with the EU fiscal rules, absence of severe macroeconomic imbalances, sustainable debt and sound policies, including the commitments made in recovery plans such as the PNRR.
explanation.shortcut: TPI = the anti-spread shield of the rate-hiking era. 'Transmission' means that rates set in Frankfurt must reach Milan and Berlin equally.
explanation.trap: Cheap funding for banks that increase lending describes the TLTROs, a different instrument introduced in 2014.
explanation.rule: The Italian spread must also be read in light of the TPI: the market prices the probability that the ECB will step in, and hence compliance with the fiscal conditions and the PNRR.

items.stem: The 'doom loop' (or sovereign-bank nexus) highlighted by the euro crisis describes which mechanism?
options: ECB rate cuts cause inflation, which then forces rate hikes that cause a recession
Sovereign stress hits the banks holding its bonds, and bank rescues hit the sovereign
Banks lend only to each other, so credit to non-financial companies dries up
Governments borrow to buy shares in their own national central bank

steps: Euro area banks hold large amounts of their own sovereign's bonds: if the spread rises, the value of those bonds falls and the banks' capital shrinks.

If the banks need help, it is the State that has to rescue them, worsening the public finances and pushing up the spread: the vicious circle feeds on itself. Ireland (2010) and Spain (2012) started from the banks, Greece and Italy from public debt.
To break it, in June 2012 euro area leaders launched banking union: single supervision by the ECB from November 2014 and a single resolution mechanism, with bail-in of creditors.
explanation.shortcut: Doom loop = two weaknesses that feed each other: a weak State weakens the banks, weak banks weaken the State.
explanation.trap: The halt in lending between banks is the 2007-08 interbank freeze: a symptom of crisis, but not the specific link between banks and the State.
explanation.rule: When you analyse an Italian bank, look at its exposure to domestic government bonds relative to its capital: it is the direct measure of the doom loop.

items.stem: Under the Recovery and Resilience Facility rules, each national plan had to devote at least what share of its total allocation to climate objectives and to the digital transition?
options: At least 20% to climate and at least 37% to digital
At least 50% to climate and at least 50% to digital
At least 37% to climate and at least 20% to digital
At least 10% to climate and at least 10% to digital

steps: The RRF regulation requires at least 37% of each plan's spending to contribute to climate objectives and at least 20% to the digital transition.
In addition, every measure must respect the principle of 'do no significant harm' to the environment (DNSH).
The six pillars of the RRF also include inclusive growth, cohesion, health and resilience, and policies for the next generation; in Italy they translate into the missions of the PNRR.
explanation.shortcut: Climate comes first and is the largest share (37), digital follows (20). Swap them and you get it wrong.
explanation.trap: The option with the percentages swapped is the most insidious: the numbers are right, the attribution is not.
explanation.rule: The green and digital quotas have steered huge public flows towards renewables, energy efficiency, networks and digitalisation: sectors on which many Italian equity stories have been built.

items.stem: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to which body of water?
options: The Red Sea
The Gulf of Oman
The Caspian Sea
The Eastern Mediterranean

steps: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and, from there, to the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean.
Under normal conditions (2024 data) around 20 million barrels a day pass through it, roughly a fifth of global oil consumption, as well as about a fifth of world LNG trade, largely from Qatar.
For Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and most of Iraq there is no real pipeline alternative; Saudi Arabia and the UAE have bypass pipelines, but with only partial capacity.
explanation.shortcut: Persian Gulf inside, Gulf of Oman outside: Hormuz is the Gulf's exit door to the Indian Ocean.
explanation.trap: The Red Sea is connected to the Indian Ocean by a different strait, Bab el-Mandeb, between Yemen and Djibouti: confusing the two chokepoints is the most common mistake.
explanation.rule: Any tension around Hormuz immediately translates into a risk premium on Brent, tanker freight rates and LNG prices: it already happened in the 1980s with the 'Tanker War' during the Iran-Iraq conflict.

items.stem: The Strait of Malacca, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, runs between which two landmasses?
options: The islands of Java and Borneo
Sri Lanka and the Indian mainland
The Malay Peninsula and Sumatra
Taiwan and mainland China

steps: The Strait of Malacca separates the Malay Peninsula (Malaysia) from the Indonesian island of Sumatra, with Singapore at its southern tip.

It connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea and is the shortest route between the Middle East, Europe and East Asia: much of the oil imported by China, Japan and South Korea passes through it.
The so-called 'Malacca dilemma' refers to China's vulnerability to a possible blockade of the strait, one of the reasons for its investment in overland pipelines and alternative ports.
explanation.shortcut: Singapore is Malacca's 'toll booth': if you remember where Singapore is, you remember the strait.
explanation.trap: The Taiwan Strait is also crucial, but it is a different route; between Sri Lanka and India lies the Palk Strait, which is shallow and not used by large ships.
explanation.rule: Malacca explains why Singapore is a hub for trading, refining and bunkering, and why the security of Asian sea lanes weighs on energy prices.

items.stem: When container ships and tankers avoid the Suez Canal and the Red Sea, which route do they typically take between Asia and Europe instead?
options: Around South America, via Cape Horn
Across the Atlantic and through the Panama Canal
Through the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz
Around Africa, via the Cape of Good Hope

steps: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, connects the Mediterranean and the Red Sea; to the south the Red Sea opens into the Gulf of Aden through the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
If the route is unsafe or blocked, ships between Asia and Europe sail around Africa via the Cape of Good Hope, adding roughly 3,000-3,500 nautical miles and about ten days of sailing.
More days at sea mean more fuel and more ships needed for the same service, and therefore higher freight rates: this is what has happened since late 2023 with the attacks on ships in the Red Sea.
explanation.shortcut: Without Suez the only sea alternative between Asia and Europe is to go around Africa: the Cape of Good Hope.
explanation.trap: Cape Horn is at the tip of South America and Panama connects the Atlantic and the Pacific in the Americas: neither is a shortcut between Asia and Europe. A detail worth knowing: the southernmost point of Africa is Cape Agulhas, but the route is named after the Cape of Good Hope.
explanation.rule: A Suez crisis translates into higher container freight rates, slower deliveries and temporary pressure on the prices of goods imported into Europe.

items.stem: Which currency accounts for the largest share of global official foreign exchange reserves reported to the IMF?
options: The euro
The Chinese renminbi
The US dollar
The Japanese yen

steps: According to the IMF's COFER data, in the 2020s the US dollar accounts for about 56-60% of allocated official foreign exchange reserves, slowly declining over the long term, while the euro accounts for about 20%.
The yen, sterling, the Canadian dollar, the Australian dollar and the renminbi follow with single-digit shares.
The dollar's dominance stems from the depth of the Treasury market, full convertibility, the rule of law and the use of the dollar to invoice commodities and trade.
explanation.shortcut: Order to remember: the dollar far ahead, the euro a distant second, then all the others with single-digit shares.
explanation.trap: The renminbi carries a lot of weight in world trade but very little in reserves, because capital controls limit its use by foreign central banks.
explanation.rule: Reserve currency status lets the US borrow more cheaply (the so-called 'exorbitant privilege') and explains why the dollar tends to appreciate in crises.

items.stem: Which article of the North Atlantic Treaty establishes that an armed attack against one NATO member is considered an attack against all members?
options: Article 4
Article 5
Article 10
Article 50

steps: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, signed in Washington in 1949, is the collective defence clause: an armed attack against one ally is considered an attack against all.
The first invocation, and as of the mid-2020s still the only one, came after the 11 September 2001 attacks on the United States.
Article 4, by contrast, provides for consultations when a member feels threatened and has been triggered several times; Article 10 governs the accession of new members.
explanation.shortcut: Five, like the fingers of a hand clenched into a fist: one for all, all for one.
explanation.trap: Article 50 is the one in the Treaty on European Union used for withdrawal (Brexit); Article 4 is consultation only, not an obligation to defend.
explanation.rule: The credibility of Article 5 underpins the debate on European defence spending, an issue that now moves public budgets and aerospace and defence stocks.

items.stem: Where is the headquarters of OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) located today?
options: Riyadh
Geneva
Baghdad
Vienna

steps: OPEC was founded in September 1960 at the Baghdad Conference by five countries: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
Its headquarters were in Geneva in the early years and since 1965 have been in Vienna, Austria, a country that is not a member of the organisation.
Since 2016 there has also been the OPEC+ format, which coordinates output with other large producers, including Russia.
explanation.shortcut: Vienna hosts many international organisations: both OPEC and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) are based there. Careful: the International Energy Agency (IEA) is based in Paris instead.
explanation.trap: Riyadh is the instinctive choice because Saudi Arabia is the most influential member, but the headquarters are in a third country; Baghdad is only where it was founded and Geneva was the first headquarters.
explanation.rule: OPEC+ meetings on production quotas are events that move the oil price, producer countries' currencies and energy stocks.

items.stem: Passage of ships through the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, the straits linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, is governed today by which international agreement?
options: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (1982)
The Treaty of Lausanne (1923)
The Treaty of Sèvres (1920)
The Montreux Convention (1936)

steps: The 1936 Montreux Convention governs transit through the Turkish Straits (Bosphorus and Dardanelles) and gives Turkey control of the straits.
In peacetime merchant ships enjoy freedom of transit; for warships, especially those of non-Black Sea states, limits apply on tonnage and length of stay.
Grain, fertilisers and oil exported from the Black Sea ports of Russia, Ukraine and, via pipeline, Kazakhstan pass through the Straits.
explanation.shortcut: Montreux = Black Sea: it is the only treaty on the list still in force that specifically governs the Turkish Straits.
explanation.trap: The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne had its own Straits regime, but it was replaced precisely by Montreux; the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea preserves straits regulated by long-standing conventions such as this one.
explanation.rule: When Turkey applies Montreux, as in 2022 when it closed the straits to warships of the belligerent countries, the Black Sea security balance shifts, and so does the risk to its grain and oil exports.

items.stem: SWIFT, the messaging network that banks use to send cross-border payment instructions, is a cooperative legally based in which country?
options: Switzerland
Belgium
United States
Luxembourg

steps: SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) is a cooperative founded in 1973 and headquartered in La Hulpe, near Brussels, Belgium.
It does not move money: it transmits standardised messages between banks, while settlement takes place through correspondent accounts and payment systems.
Because it is subject to Belgian and EU law, the exclusions of banks from SWIFT (Iranian banks in 2012, several Russian banks in 2022) were decided through European Union regulations.
