explanation.shortcut: The name sounds Swiss, but SWIFT is Belgian: think of Brussels, home of the EU institutions that decide its sanctions.
explanation.trap: Switzerland tempts because of the similar sound and its banking tradition; the United States tempts because the dollar dominates payments, but SWIFT is not an American institution.
explanation.rule: Disconnection from SWIFT is one of the most powerful financial sanctions because it makes a country's international payments slow and costly, with effects on exports, the currency and correspondent banks.

items.stem: The acronym BRIC was coined in 2001 for Brazil, Russia, India and China. Which country was invited to join the group in 2010, turning it into BRICS?
options: Nigeria
Mexico
Turkey
South Africa

steps: The term BRIC was coined in 2001 in a report by an investment bank economist to describe the large emerging economies set to grow rapidly.
The four countries began meeting at formal summits in 2009; South Africa was invited in 2010 and attended the 2011 summit, hence the final 'S'.
Since 2024 the group has expanded to other countries, including Middle Eastern energy producers, and discusses trade in local currencies and alternatives to the dollar.
explanation.shortcut: The final S stands for South Africa: it is the only African country in the original group of five.
explanation.trap: Mexico, Nigeria and Turkey are large emerging economies named in another acronym (MINT, with Indonesia), but they did not join the group in 2010.
explanation.rule: The BRICS matter for demographics, commodities and trade, but remain heterogeneous: a real alternative to the dollar requires open and deep capital markets, which are lacking today.

items.stem: Before 2022, roughly what share of the European Union's natural gas imports came from Russia?
options: About 10%
About 40%
About 70%
About 90%

steps: In 2021 Russia supplied about 40-45% of EU gas imports, mostly by pipeline.
Dependence varied widely: some Central and Eastern European countries relied almost entirely on Russian gas, while the Iberian Peninsula was supplied mainly by North Africa and LNG.
After 2022 the EU replaced most of those volumes with Norwegian pipeline gas and with LNG, mainly from the US, while also cutting consumption.
explanation.shortcut: Think 'almost half': enough to cause an energy crisis in 2022, but not all of it, because Norway, North Africa and LNG covered the rest.
explanation.trap: 90% is true only for some individual countries, not for the EU as a whole: confusing a single country's figure with the bloc's is a classic mistake.
explanation.rule: The 2022 gas crisis showed that energy security is industrial competitiveness: higher gas prices weigh on the margins of European chemicals, steel and manufacturing.

items.stem: The G7 price cap on Russian seaborne crude oil, introduced in December 2022, mainly works by:
options: Banning every country in the world from buying Russian crude oil
Setting a floor price below which Russia may not sell its crude
Barring G7 and EU firms from insuring or shipping cargoes sold above it
Imposing a tariff on Russian crude, collected by G7 customs authorities

steps: The price cap does not prohibit third countries from buying Russian oil: it prohibits G7 and EU companies from providing services (shipping, insurance, financing, brokerage) for cargoes sold above the maximum price, initially set at $60 a barrel.
The idea is to exploit the dominant role of Western insurers and shipowners to keep the barrels on the market, avoiding a supply shock, while cutting Russian revenues.
The response was the growth of the so-called 'shadow fleet' of tankers with opaque ownership and non-Western insurance.
explanation.shortcut: Price cap = a sanction on services, not on the barrel: it hits those who insure and ship, not those who buy.
explanation.trap: A total ban looks like the 'toughest' option, but the aim was the opposite: not to take oil off the world market, so as not to send prices soaring.
explanation.rule: Modern sanctions aim to hit a country's revenues without destabilising markets: understanding the mechanism helps you read the discounts between crudes (e.g. Urals versus Brent) and the compliance risks for banks and insurers.

items.stem: Why can a severe drought force the Panama Canal to limit the number and the draft of ships passing through?
options: Its locks run on fresh water from a rain-fed lake, drained with each transit
It is a sea-level canal, so a drought lowers the water level of both oceans
Drought triggers sandstorms that fill the shipping channel with sand and silt
Insurers suspend cover for canal transits during a declared drought

steps: The Panama Canal, opened in 1914, is not at sea level: ships are raised and lowered by locks fed with fresh water from Gatún Lake, an artificial lake fed by rainfall.
Each transit discharges a large amount of fresh water into the sea; during droughts the lake level drops and the canal authority reduces daily transits and maximum draught.
This happened in 2023, a year of severe drought linked to El Niño, with queues of ships and auctions for transit slots.
explanation.shortcut: Suez is a sea-level canal, Panama is a 'water lift': without rain the lift stops.
explanation.trap: Many think Panama works like Suez, at sea level; in fact the system of locks and a lake makes the canal dependent on the climate.
explanation.rule: Climate risk is also logistics risk: restrictions at Panama mainly hit routes between Asia and the US East Coast and US exports of LNG and grain.

items.stem: Which provision of the EU treaties contains the mutual assistance clause for a member state that is the victim of armed aggression on its territory, invoked for the first time by France in November 2015?
options: Article 50 TEU
Article 222 TFEU
Article 42(7) TEU
Article 7 TEU

steps: Article 42, paragraph 7, of the Treaty on European Union obliges the other Member States to provide aid and assistance by all the means in their power to a Member State that is the victim of armed aggression.
France invoked it for the first time after the Paris attacks of 13 November 2015.
The clause is without prejudice to NATO commitments and to the specific character of neutral states' defence policies, so it does not replace NATO's Article 5.
explanation.shortcut: 42(7) TEU is the EU's 'defence clause', in the chapter on the common security and defence policy; 222 TFEU is the solidarity clause for terrorism and disasters.
explanation.trap: Article 222 TFEU looks like a good fit because it also covers terrorist attacks, but it is the Union's solidarity clause; France chose 42(7), which refers to armed aggression and commits the Member States.
explanation.rule: The debate on European defence (spending, joint procurement, defence debt) rests on these legal bases, which now move public budgets and industry.

items.stem: In the context of US sanctions, what distinguishes 'secondary sanctions' from primary sanctions?
options: They hit non-US firms dealing with the sanctioned party, threatening their US access
They are adopted by the UN Security Council rather than by a single country
They take effect only after primary sanctions have been in force for at least a year
They apply only to state-owned enterprises of the sanctioned country

steps: Primary sanctions prohibit US persons (citizens, companies, transactions that go through the US financial system) from doing business with the sanctioned party.

Secondary sanctions, by contrast, target non-US persons, for example a European or Asian bank, that do business with the sanctioned party: the risk is losing access to the US market and financial system.
They are largely administered by OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control) of the US Treasury; for an international bank, losing access to the dollar is an existential risk.
explanation.shortcut: Primary: 'you, an American, cannot'. Secondary: 'you, a foreigner, if you do it you lose America'.
explanation.trap: UN sanctions are multilateral and bind all Member States, but they are not 'secondary': the distinction is about who is targeted, not who decides.
explanation.rule: The extraterritorial reach of US sanctions explains why European banks have very strict compliance and why sanctions due diligence is part of every cross-border deal.

items.stem: The 'Triffin dilemma', described by the economist Robert Triffin around 1960, refers to the conflict faced by the issuer of the world's main reserve currency between:
options: Keeping inflation low and keeping unemployment low at the same time
Fixing the exchange rate, allowing free capital flows and setting its own rates
Cutting taxes to boost growth and reducing public debt in the same period
Supplying the world with its currency through deficits and keeping trust in it

steps: Under the Bretton Woods system the rest of the world used the dollar as a reserve: to supply enough dollars the United States had to run balance of payments deficits.

But the more dollars accumulated abroad relative to US gold reserves, the less credible convertibility at $35 an ounce became: providing liquidity to the world eroded confidence in the currency itself.

The tensions culminated in August 1971 with the suspension of gold convertibility; in a different form the issue resurfaces today in the debate on US external deficits and the global role of the dollar.
explanation.shortcut: Triffin = liquidity versus confidence: the more currency you give the world, the more you risk the world ceasing to trust it.
explanation.trap: A fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and independent monetary policy form the Mundell-Fleming 'trilemma' (or impossible trinity): a different concept, which applies to any country and not only to the issuer of the reserve currency.
explanation.rule: Being the reserve currency brings advantages (cheaper funding) but requires supplying the world with safe assets in ever larger quantities: it is the key to reading the debate on the future of the dollar.

items.stem: As of the mid-2020s, which country is the world's largest producer of mined copper?
options: China
Chile
Australia
Canada

steps: Chile has for decades been the world's largest producer of mined copper, with about a quarter of global output; in the mid-2020s it is followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is growing strongly, and Peru.
China, by contrast, is the largest consumer and the largest refiner of copper: it imports large quantities of concentrate and turns it into refined copper.
Copper is essential for power grids, construction, electric vehicles and data centres, which is why its price is seen as a gauge of the industrial cycle ('Dr. Copper').
explanation.shortcut: Copper = the Andes: Chile is the first answer to consider, with Congo as the fast-growing second producer.
explanation.trap: China dominates refining and consumption, not mining: confusing who extracts with who processes is the typical commodities mistake.
explanation.rule: The Chilean peso tends to move with the copper price, and the energy transition makes copper a strategic commodity for utilities, autos and infrastructure.

items.stem: As of the mid-2020s, which country is the world's largest economy measured by nominal GDP in US dollars?
options: China
Japan
Germany
United States

steps: At current prices and market exchange rates the United States is the world's largest economy, with about a quarter of global GDP; China is second.
Measured at purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts for different price levels, China is instead the largest economy according to the IMF since the mid-2010s.
Germany, Japan and India follow at a distance; in nominal rankings the middle positions often change, partly because of exchange rate effects.
explanation.shortcut: Nominal = US, PPP = China: remember them as a pair.
explanation.trap: China is the tempting answer because it ranks first in PPP and in goods exports, but the question asks for nominal GDP in dollars.
explanation.rule: When you quote an economic ranking, always specify the metric (nominal, PPP, per capita): it is a detail an interviewer notices immediately.

items.stem: The so-called 'lithium triangle', which holds a large share of the world's identified lithium resources in salt flats, spans which countries?
options: Argentina, Bolivia and Chile
Australia, China and Chile
Peru, Ecuador and Colombia
Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay

steps: The 'lithium triangle' covers the salares (salt flats) of Argentina, Bolivia and Chile on the Andean plateau, where lithium is extracted from brines evaporated in large ponds.
The largest lithium producer, however, is Australia, which obtains it from hard rock (spodumene), while most refining into battery products takes place in China.
Demand for lithium is driven by batteries for electric vehicles and stationary storage, and its price has been extremely volatile in recent years.
explanation.shortcut: Triangle = three neighbours in the Andes: Chile, Argentina, Bolivia.
explanation.trap: Australia, China and Chile are the main producers or refiners, but the 'triangle' is a geographical resource concept, not a production ranking.
explanation.rule: Distinguishing resources, production and refining is essential to assess the supply chain risks of critical raw materials.

items.stem: Which country dominates the global supply of rare earth elements, especially at the processing and refining stage?
options: United States
Australia
China
Brazil

steps: China mines most of the world's rare earths and controls an even higher share, around 90%, of separation, refining and permanent magnet production.
Rare earths are used in magnets for electric motors and wind turbines, in electronics and in defence systems.
In recent years China has introduced export controls on some critical raw materials, and the US, the EU, Japan and Australia are trying to develop alternative supply chains.
explanation.shortcut: For critical raw materials always ask who refines, not just who mines: for rare earths the answer is China.
explanation.trap: The United States and Australia have active mines and Brazil has large reserves, but without comparable refining capacity they remain dependent on the Chinese supply chain.
explanation.rule: The concentration of refining is a geopolitical risk that feeds into valuations of sectors such as autos, defence and renewable energy.

items.stem: According to the BIS Triennial Central Bank Survey, which country hosts the largest share of global foreign exchange trading?
options: United States
Singapore
Hong Kong SAR
United Kingdom

steps: The triennial survey of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has shown since its early editions that the United Kingdom, i.e. London, is the leading centre for FX trading: in the 2022 survey its share was around 38% of the global total, roughly double that of the United States.
The United States, Singapore and Hong Kong follow; London's advantage stems from its time zone, English law and the concentration of international banks.
London is also a leading centre for over-the-counter interest rate derivatives and for the international debt market.
explanation.shortcut: London's time zone 'stitches together' the market day: in the morning it talks to Asia, in the afternoon to New York.
explanation.trap: New York is the capital of equity markets and Treasuries, but in FX trading London is clearly first.
explanation.rule: If you are aiming for a graduate programme in London, being able to explain why the City remains central for FX, derivatives and international debt even after Brexit is an interview-ready answer.

items.stem: Since 2017, which country has been the world's largest importer of crude oil?
options: United States
China
India
Japan

steps: China overtook the United States as the largest annual importer of crude oil in 2017 and in the 2020s imports more than 10 million barrels a day, over 70% of its needs.
The United States, thanks to shale, has become the world's largest producer and imports less; India is the third major importer.
Chinese demand is therefore one of the main drivers of the oil price and of tanker flows through Hormuz and Malacca.
explanation.shortcut: The country with the largest manufacturing industry and little oil of its own imports the most: China.
explanation.trap: The United States was long the largest importer, but shale reversed its position: today it is the largest producer.
explanation.rule: Data on Chinese crude imports and refinery utilisation are indicators that markets follow to gauge global demand.

items.stem: As of 2024, which country is the world's largest producer of crude oil?
options: Saudi Arabia
Russia
United States
Canada

steps: Since 2018 the United States has been the world's largest crude producer, thanks to shale oil extracted with horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, mainly in the Permian Basin.
In 2024 US crude output exceeded 13 million barrels a day, an all-time record.
Saudi Arabia remains the largest crude exporter and the country with the most spare capacity, which gives it the role of 'swing producer' within OPEC+.
explanation.shortcut: Largest producer = US (shale); largest exporter and swing producer = Saudi Arabia.
explanation.trap: Saudi Arabia is the instinctive answer because it is the face of OPEC, but it produces less than the US, partly because of the cuts agreed within OPEC+.
explanation.rule: US shale responds to prices relatively quickly, so it limits lasting oil price rallies and reduces the market power of OPEC+.

items.stem: In 2024, which three countries were the world's largest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG)?
options: Russia, Norway and Algeria
Saudi Arabia, Iran and Iraq
Canada, Brazil and Mexico
The US, Qatar and Australia

steps: In 2024 the three largest LNG exporters were the United States, Australia and Qatar, together about 60% of world exports; the US became the largest exporter in 2023 thanks to shale gas.

Qatar shares the world's largest gas field with Iran (North Field for Qatar, South Pars for Iran), but all its LNG must pass through Hormuz: every crisis in the strait puts a significant share of world supply at risk.
Norway is a major supplier to Europe, but mainly by pipeline; Russia and Algeria export a lot of gas, largely by pipeline.
explanation.shortcut: LNG = plenty of gas and customers reachable only by ship: the US (shale), Qatar (North Field) and Australia, separated from its Asian customers by sea.
explanation.trap: Russia, Norway and Algeria are large gas exporters to Europe, but mostly by pipeline, which does not count as LNG.
explanation.rule: LNG has made the gas market more global: European (TTF) and Asian (JKM) prices compete for the same cargoes, and Europe depends more on US supplies.

items.stem: Since the late 2010s, which country has generally been the world's largest exporter of wheat?
options: United States
China
Russia
India

steps: Russia has been the world's largest wheat exporter since the late 2010s, with volumes above those of the United States, Canada and Australia.
China and India are among the largest producers, but they consume almost everything domestically and India often restricts exports to contain domestic prices.
Before 2022 Russia and Ukraine together accounted for about a quarter or more of world wheat exports, with the Middle East and North Africa among the main buyers.
explanation.shortcut: Producing a lot is not enough to export: what counts is the surplus. Russia has the largest surplus, thanks to the 'black earth' of the south.
explanation.trap: China and India are tempting because they are the largest producers, but with over a billion people each they have no large surpluses to export.
explanation.rule: The wheat price affects food inflation and the political stability of many importing countries: a shock in the Black Sea is a macro and geopolitical risk.

items.stem: Which country produces roughly 70% or more of the world's mined cobalt, a key input for many lithium-ion batteries?
options: DR Congo
Indonesia
Australia
Chile

steps: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) mines over 70% of the world's cobalt, often as a by-product of copper mining.
Indonesia has grown rapidly into the second-largest producer thanks to nickel processing, while cobalt refining takes place largely in China.
Concentration in a country with governance risks, together with concerns about working conditions in artisanal mines, is pushing battery makers to reduce cobalt content.
explanation.shortcut: Cobalt = Congo: same first letters, 'Co'.
explanation.trap: Indonesia is the second-largest producer and is growing, but it dominates nickel, not cobalt.
explanation.rule: For a concentrated commodity, country risk, ESG and control of the refining supply chain matter as much as the spot price.

items.stem: Which country is the world's largest exporter of soybeans, with China as its main customer?
options: Brazil
United States
Argentina
Canada

steps: In the 2020s Brazil is the world's largest producer and exporter of soybeans, with a widening lead over the United States.
China imports about 60% of the soybeans traded worldwide, mainly as animal feed for pig farming.
Argentina matters mainly as an exporter of soybean meal and oil, i.e. products that have already been processed.
explanation.shortcut: Soybeans = Brazil + China: the first grows them, the second feeds them to its livestock.
explanation.trap: The United States was long the top exporter and remains second; its share of sales to China has also fallen because of trade tensions.
explanation.rule: US-China trade wars are also fought over agricultural products: tariffs on American soybeans shift demand towards Brazil and move prices and freight rates.

items.stem: In recent decades, roughly half or more of the world's cocoa has been grown in two neighbouring West African countries. Which ones?
options: Nigeria and Cameroon
Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana
Senegal and Mali
Ghana and Togo

steps: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer, with about 40% of the total; Ghana is traditionally second, although its output has fallen in recent seasons and Ecuador has closed the gap.
Geographical concentration makes supply vulnerable to weather, crop disease and government policy, since in both countries the state sets or influences the prices paid to farmers.
In 2024 poor harvests in West Africa pushed cocoa prices to record highs, affecting chocolate makers' margins and list prices.
explanation.shortcut: The two neighbours on the Gulf of Guinea: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana.
explanation.trap: Nigeria and Cameroon produce cocoa but with much smaller shares; Togo borders Ghana but its output is marginal.
explanation.rule: Agricultural commodities concentrated in a few countries generate sudden price shocks, which feed through to the margins, hedging and working capital of food companies.

items.stem: Which country became by far the world's largest producer of nickel, helped by a ban on exports of unprocessed nickel ore that pushed smelting and refining onshore?
options: Philippines
Russia
Canada
Indonesia

steps: Indonesia produces over half of the world's nickel; since 2020 it has banned exports of raw ore, forcing it to be processed in the country.
The ban attracted huge investment, largely Chinese, in smelters and processing plants, turning the country into a hub of the stainless steel and battery supply chains.
Rising Indonesian supply has depressed nickel prices and put mines in other countries under pressure.
explanation.shortcut: The textbook case of 'downstreaming': ban exports of raw ore and force the added value to stay at home. Think Indonesia.
explanation.trap: The Philippines is the second-largest producer but exports mainly raw ore; Russia has historically been important for high-grade nickel, but with far smaller volumes.
explanation.rule: Resource nationalism (export bans, royalties, local processing requirements) is a key risk for anyone financing or valuing mining companies.

items.stem: According to OPEC and most widely used industry statistics, which country holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves?
options: Venezuela
Saudi Arabia
Russia
United States

steps: Venezuela reports the world's largest proven oil reserves, about 300 billion barrels, mostly extra-heavy crude from the Orinoco Belt.
Saudi Arabia is second; Canada also has huge reserves thanks to its oil sands.
Despite its reserves, Venezuelan production has collapsed over recent decades because of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.
explanation.shortcut: Reserves are not production: 'who has the most oil underground' is Venezuela, 'who extracts the most' is the US.
explanation.trap: Saudi Arabia is the knee-jerk answer, but it is second; Venezuelan reserves are heavy and costly to extract, which is why they do not translate into production.
explanation.rule: When valuing energy assets, what matters is economically recoverable value, not the declared volume: extraction cost, crude quality and country risk make the difference.

items.stem: The world's largest sovereign wealth fund, which on average owns around 1.5% of all listed shares globally, was built from which country's petroleum revenues?
options: Saudi Arabia
United Arab Emirates
Norway
Kuwait

steps: Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, fed by oil and gas revenues, is the world's largest sovereign wealth fund and invests exclusively outside Norway.
On average it holds about 1.5% of all listed companies in the world, plus bonds, real estate and renewable infrastructure; it is managed by a division of the Norwegian central bank.
A fiscal rule allows the government to spend about 3% of the fund's value each year, equal to the expected real return, preserving the capital for future generations.
explanation.shortcut: Oil + strong institutions + a spending rule = Norway, the textbook example of how to avoid the 'resource curse'.
explanation.trap: The Gulf funds (Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia) are huge and very active in dealmaking, but the largest by assets is Norway's; Kuwait's, on the other hand, is the oldest.
explanation.rule: Sovereign wealth funds are among the largest investors and co-investors in M&A and equity offerings: understanding their logic is useful for any banker.

items.stem: For a commercial bank, net interest margin (NIM) is calculated as:
options: Net income divided by average shareholders' equity
Operating expenses divided by operating income
Net interest income over average earning assets
Total loans divided by total deposits

steps: NIM is net interest income (interest income minus interest expense) divided by average interest-earning assets: it measures how much the bank earns on transforming funding into lending.
For a commercial bank net interest income is often the largest revenue line; a typical NIM is in the order of a few percentage points, lower in Europe than in the United States.
The other options describe other key metrics: ROE, cost/income ratio and loan-to-deposit ratio.
explanation.shortcut: NIM = how much each euro of interest-earning assets yields: net interest income in the numerator, interest-earning assets in the denominator.
explanation.trap: ROE (net income / equity) is the most quoted profitability metric, but it measures the return to shareholders, not the margin on lending.
explanation.rule: When you analyse a bank, start from NIM, cost/income, cost of risk and CET1: together they explain almost all of the income statement and the bank's soundness.

items.stem: A property and casualty insurer reports a combined ratio of 103%. What does this mean?
options: Claims and expenses exceeded earned premiums: an underwriting loss
Its investment portfolio delivered a 3% return during the year
Its solvency capital exceeds the regulatory minimum by 3%
Its gross written premiums grew by 3% compared with the prior year

steps: Combined ratio = (claims + expenses) / earned premiums: it is the sum of the loss ratio and the expense ratio.
Below 100% the insurer makes money on underwriting; above 100%, as here, it spends 103 for every 100 of premiums.
It can still report a profit thanks to the return on investments made with the 'float', i.e. premiums collected before claims are paid.
explanation.shortcut: Read the combined ratio as the cost per 100 euros of premium: above 100 the insurance business itself is losing money.
explanation.trap: The 3% looks like a return or growth because it is a positive number, but here it indicates costs in excess of premiums.
explanation.rule: For a P&C insurer the combined ratio is the key metric: comparing it across peers and over time reveals pricing discipline and portfolio quality.

items.stem: In the airline industry, 'load factor' measures:
options: The share of available seat capacity filled by paying passengers
Fuel costs as a share of the airline's total operating costs
The average fare paid per passenger on each flight
The share of flights that depart and arrive on schedule

steps: Load factor = RPK / ASK, i.e. revenue passenger kilometres divided by available seat kilometres: it shows what percentage of the capacity offered has been sold.
Airlines have very high fixed costs (aircraft, crews, slots), so each additional point of load factor largely drops through to margin; values around 80-85% are common for efficient carriers.
It should be read together with yield (revenue per passenger kilometre): filling the aircraft with fares that are too low does not create value.
explanation.shortcut: Load factor = how full the aircraft is, weighted by distance.
explanation.trap: Fuel as a share of costs is an important metric for airlines, but it is not the load factor.
explanation.rule: In all fixed-capacity businesses (airlines, hotels, cruises) the key metric is the occupancy rate multiplied by the average price.

items.stem: Why do retailers report 'like-for-like' (same-store) sales growth alongside total sales growth?
options: To show growth including the contribution of newly opened stores
To comply with a legal requirement to report sales by country
To measure the growth of online and mobile app sales on their own
To isolate growth at existing stores, excluding openings and closures

steps: Like-for-like (LFL) sales compare only stores open in both periods, usually for at least 12 months, excluding openings, closures and often currency effects.
A retailer can grow total revenue by opening many stores even if existing ones are selling less: LFL exposes this situation.
LFL is often broken down into traffic (number of transactions) and average basket, to understand whether growth comes from volumes or from prices.
explanation.shortcut: LFL = same perimeter: you compare apples with apples.
explanation.trap: Total growth includes new openings, which is exactly what LFL aims to exclude; negative LFL alongside growing revenue is a warning sign.
explanation.rule: Whenever you see revenue growth, ask how much is organic and how much comes from scope, price or currency.

items.stem: For a software-as-a-service (SaaS) company, ARR stands for:
options: Adjusted Revenue Recognition, revenue recognised after releasing deferred income
Average Revenue Rate, total revenue divided by the number of products
Annual Recurring Revenue, the annualised value of active subscription contracts
Accumulated Reinvestment Ratio, the share of profits reinvested

steps: ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) is the annualised value of active subscription contracts at a given date, often calculated as MRR (monthly recurring revenue) times 12.
It excludes non-recurring revenue such as implementation or consulting, and it is a management metric, not an accounting standard.
Investors use it together with churn and net revenue retention to assess revenue growth and quality; many SaaS companies are valued on EV/ARR multiples.
explanation.shortcut: ARR = a snapshot of subscription revenue over the next 12 months, if nobody cancels and nobody buys more.
explanation.trap: The option mentioning 'revenue recognition' sounds technical, but ARR is not an IFRS or GAAP accounting figure: it is an operating KPI.
explanation.rule: In software, revenue quality (recurring, predictable, with low churn) justifies much higher multiples than businesses with one-off revenue.

items.stem: A telecom operator's ARPU is typically calculated as:
options: Service revenue divided by the average number of subscribers
EBITDA divided by the number of mobile towers in its network
New subscribers added divided by the total subscriber base
Total capex divided by the number of subscribers at year end

steps: ARPU (Average Revenue Per User) is service revenue divided by the average number of customers in the period, usually expressed on a monthly basis.
In telecoms, revenue equals customers times ARPU; in mature, saturated markets growth comes mainly from price increases, richer data plans and converged fixed-mobile offers.
It is analysed together with churn (the rate at which customers leave) and capex intensity (capex / revenue), because networks require continuous investment.
explanation.shortcut: ARPU = how much each customer pays on average per month: revenue / average customers.
explanation.trap: The ratio of new customers to the total is an acquisition rate, a different metric; costs and EBITDA do not enter ARPU, which is a revenue measure.
explanation.rule: In a mature sector an ARPU that holds up despite competition signals pricing power; falling ARPU with a stable customer base signals a price war.

items.stem: For a regulated network utility, such as an electricity grid or a water company in the UK, allowed revenues are set by the regulator mainly on the basis of:
options: Its share of the national retail electricity or water market
Last year's dividend payments to shareholders, grown in line with inflation
The regulated asset base times an allowed return, plus allowed costs
The average spot price of electricity on the wholesale market

steps: Electricity, gas and water networks are natural monopolies: the regulator sets allowed revenues for a multi-year period (price control).
Basic formula: allowed revenues ≈ RAB × allowed return (regulatory WACC) + regulatory depreciation + allowed operating costs, with the RAB often indexed to inflation.
Approved investment increases the RAB and therefore future revenues: RAB growth is the main driver of these companies' earnings.
explanation.shortcut: Regulated utility = 'I grant you a return on what you have invested in the network': RAB times allowed WACC.
explanation.trap: The spot price of electricity matters for power generators, not for regulated networks, which are remunerated regardless of wholesale prices.
explanation.rule: To value a regulated utility, look at RAB growth, the allowed return relative to the actual cost of capital, and the debt/RAB ratio (gearing).

items.stem: Which factor best explains why leading luxury brands can sustain very high gross margins and raise prices above inflation without losing much demand?
options: Brand desirability and scarcity, backed by tight control of distribution
Much lower raw material and labour costs than those of mass-market brands
Government rules that set minimum retail prices for luxury goods
High-volume sales through outlet stores and online discount channels

steps: In luxury the price is part of the product: brand desirability, heritage and perceived scarcity allow prices to rise while demand stays relatively insensitive (pricing power).
The big brands protect this power by controlling distribution (directly operated stores, few wholesalers), avoiding sales and limiting supply.
The result is gross margins often above 60% for the strongest brands; the metrics to watch are organic growth, price/volume mix and the share of sales through direct channels.
explanation.shortcut: In luxury, discounting destroys value: a brand that never holds sales has pricing power.
explanation.trap: Low costs do not explain such high margins: many luxury products in fact use expensive materials and craftsmanship; the margin comes from the price.
explanation.rule: Pricing power is the first quality an investor looks for in a business: it protects margins from inflation and justifies high multiples.

items.stem: A SaaS company reports net revenue retention (NRR) of 120%. What does this mean?
options: It added 20% more new customers than in the previous year
Revenue from year-ago customers is up 20%, net of churn and downgrades
Total revenue, including revenue from newly acquired customers, grew 20%
Only 80% of its customers renewed their contracts this year

steps: NRR takes the cohort of customers from 12 months ago and compares their recurring revenue today with what it was then, adding expansion (upsell, more users) and subtracting downgrades and lost customers (churn).
120% means that, even without acquiring a single new customer, recurring revenue would grow by 20%: expansion comfortably exceeds losses.
Gross revenue retention (GRR), by contrast, excludes expansion and therefore cannot exceed 100%.
explanation.shortcut: NRR = growth from a constant customer base: new customers never enter the calculation.
explanation.trap: Total revenue growth includes new customers, which NRR excludes by definition: a company can have high NRR and lower total growth, or vice versa.
explanation.rule: NRR above 100% points to a product that becomes more indispensable over time; together with the 'Rule of 40' (growth % + margin % ≥ 40) it is one of the first numbers a software investor looks at.

items.stem: When policy rates rise, what typically happens to the net interest margin of a bank whose loans are mostly floating rate and whose deposits reprice slowly?
options: It widens, because loan yields reprice faster than deposit costs
It narrows, because deposit costs rise immediately one-for-one with rates
It stays unchanged, because assets and liabilities move together
It narrows, because borrowers repay their floating-rate loans early

steps: If loans are floating rate, their yield rises almost immediately with reference rates (for example Euribor).
Sight deposits, on the other hand, adjust slowly and only partially: the share of the rate rise passed on to depositors is called 'deposit beta' and is low in the early stages of a hiking cycle.
The result is an expanding NIM, as for European banks in 2023-2024; when rates fall the effect reverses.
explanation.shortcut: Rates up: floating-rate assets reprice immediately, liabilities are sticky, so the margin rises.
explanation.trap: Assuming that deposits follow rates immediately, one for one: in reality banks raise the rates paid on accounts with a lag, until competition forces them to.
explanation.rule: The sensitivity of net interest income to rates (NII sensitivity) is one of the first numbers analysts ask banks for when the monetary cycle turns.

items.stem: Why do analysts often look at an airline's CASK 'ex-fuel' (cost per available seat kilometre excluding fuel)?
options: Fuel is a large, volatile cost that management largely cannot control
Fuel is not recorded as an operating expense under IFRS
All airlines pay exactly the same price for their jet fuel
Regulators require listed airlines to report their unit costs excluding fuel

steps: CASK = operating costs / available seat kilometres (ASK): it measures how much it costs to offer one seat for one kilometre; RASK is the equivalent on the revenue side.
Fuel accounts for a significant share of an airline's costs, often between a fifth and a third, and depends on oil, the dollar and hedging more than on management efficiency.
CASK ex-fuel isolates staff, maintenance, airport charges and fleet costs: it is the key measure for comparing low-cost and legacy models.
explanation.shortcut: Strip out what management does not control to see what it does control: the same logic as 'core' or 'underlying'.
explanation.trap: Fuel is, to all intents and purposes, an operating cost in the accounts: it is excluded for analysis, not under accounting rules.
explanation.rule: The difference between RASK and CASK is the unit margin: low-cost carriers win with a structurally lower CASK, legacy carriers rely on a higher RASK.

items.stem: Why do large grocery retailers often operate with negative working capital?
options: They hold large stocks of slow-moving goods in their warehouses
Tax rules let them defer VAT payments to the state indefinitely
They sell stock quickly for cash but pay suppliers on longer terms
They offer long payment terms to their retail customers

steps: Operating working capital ≈ trade receivables + inventory - trade payables.
A supermarket is paid immediately (cash or card, almost no receivables), turns its inventory in a few weeks and pays suppliers at 30-60 days or more: payables exceed receivables and inventory.
In effect, suppliers finance the business: growth generates cash instead of absorbing it, but a fall in sales drains cash quickly.
explanation.shortcut: Collect before you pay = negative working capital = suppliers acting as the bank.
explanation.trap: Lots of inventory would increase working capital, not reduce it; and grocery retailers do not extend credit to end customers.
explanation.rule: In valuation and LBO models negative working capital is a source of cash, but it needs scrutiny: stretching supplier payments is not sustainable growth.

items.stem: Basel III added a leverage ratio, with a minimum of 3%, alongside the risk-based capital requirements. How is it calculated?
options: CET1 capital divided by risk-weighted assets, including buffers
Tier 1 capital divided by total exposures, with no risk weighting
High-quality liquid assets divided by 30-day stressed net outflows
Total shareholders' equity divided by total customer deposits

steps: Leverage ratio = Tier 1 capital / total exposure (on-balance-sheet assets plus certain off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures), with no risk weighting at all; the Basel III minimum is 3%.

It was introduced after 2008 because many banks had reassuring capital ratios but enormous leverage: assets with low risk weights, often calculated with internal models, concealed the true level of indebtedness.

It works as a 'backstop': a simple constraint that is hard to get around, limiting leverage even when risk weights underestimate risk; global systemically important banks face an additional specific buffer.
explanation.shortcut: Leverage ratio = capital over 'naked' assets, without risk weights: a 3% minimum means at most about 33 euros of exposure for every euro of Tier 1.
explanation.trap: High-quality liquid assets over 30-day net outflows is the Liquidity Coverage Ratio, a liquidity requirement rather than a capital one; CET1 over RWA is the risk-weighted ratio, i.e. precisely the measure that the leverage ratio complements.
explanation.rule: Read a bank through two lenses: the CET1 ratio measures capital against estimated risk, the leverage ratio against the size of the balance sheet; if the binding constraint is the latter, high-volume, low-risk activities (repo, government bonds) become expensive.

items.stem: A subscription business loses 2% of its customers every month and adds no new ones. Roughly what share of its starting customers remains after 12 months?
options: About 76%
About 78%
About 82%
About 98%

steps: Monthly churn compounds: customers remaining = (1 - 0.02)^12 = 0.98^12.

Quick calculation by squaring: 0.98^2 ≈ 0.960; 0.98^4 ≈ 0.922; 0.98^8 ≈ 0.851; 0.98^12 = 0.98^8 × 0.98^4 ≈ 0.851 × 0.922 ≈ 0.785. About 78% of customers remain, i.e. an effective annual churn of 21-22%.

The linear calculation 12 × 2% = 24% (76% remaining) overstates the losses, because each month the 2% applies to an already reduced base; 98%, on the other hand, is the mistake of looking at a single month.
explanation.shortcut: For small rates (1 - x)^n ≈ e^(-n·x), slightly above 1 - n·x: e^(-0.24) ≈ 0.79, so the answer is just above the linear 76%.
explanation.trap: 76% is the result of the linear calculation (12 × 2%): the most common mistake is forgetting compounding.
explanation.rule: A monthly churn that looks small (2%) means losing over a fifth of customers a year: in SaaS and telecoms retention is worth as much as acquisition.

items.stem: A listed regulated water utility trades at an enterprise value of 1.1x its regulated asset base (RAB). What does this premium most likely imply?
options: Its RAB is overstated by about 10% in the company's accounts
The regulator has just announced a 10% cut to the company's allowed revenues
The company is close to breaching its bank debt covenants
Investors expect it to earn more than its cost of capital on the RAB

steps: If a utility earned on its RAB exactly the return required by investors, its enterprise value would tend to be close to 1.0x RAB.

A premium (1.1x) indicates that the market expects more: an allowed return above the actual cost of capital, cost savings relative to the regulator's assumptions, performance incentives or RAB growth at attractive returns.
A discount to RAB, by contrast, signals fears of penalties, allowed returns that are too low or balance sheet problems.
explanation.shortcut: EV/RAB is the 'price-to-book' of utilities: above 1 the market believes the invested capital earns more than it costs.
explanation.trap: Thinking that the premium indicates an accounting error: the RAB is a regulatory value, and the premium reflects expectations about future returns, not an overvaluation of the asset.
explanation.rule: The same principle applies everywhere: a multiple above book or regulatory value is justified only if the return on capital exceeds its cost.

items.stem: In its commonly cited form, Moore's law states that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every:
options: Six months
Two years
Five years
Ten years

steps: In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors per chip was doubling roughly every year; in 1975 he revised the estimate to roughly every two years, the version most often quoted today.
It is not a law of physics but an empirical observation that for decades guided the industry's roadmap: more transistors mean more powerful chips and a lower cost per transistor.
In recent years the pace has slowed and the cost of each new manufacturing generation has risen sharply, so progress increasingly comes from specialised architectures and advanced packaging.
explanation.shortcut: Doubling every two years means roughly 1,000 times in twenty years (2^10 ≈ 1,024).
explanation.trap: Six months is too fast; you sometimes hear '18 months', which refers more to performance than to transistor count: the standard formulation is two years.
explanation.rule: The slowdown in Moore's law explains why the semiconductor industry is ever more capital intensive and concentrated, and why chips have become a geopolitical issue.

items.stem: At its core, how does a large language model (LLM) generate text?
options: By retrieving pre-written answers stored in a large database
By applying grammar rules hand-coded by teams of linguists
By searching the internet in real time for every sentence it writes
By repeatedly predicting a likely next token given the text so far

steps: An LLM is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token (a word or a fragment of a word) given the preceding context.

By generating one token at a time and feeding it back into the context, it produces sentences and reasoning; subsequent training with human feedback and other methods makes it more useful and safer as an assistant.
Some systems can be connected to search engines or company documents (retrieval), but the underlying mechanism remains next-token prediction.
explanation.shortcut: Think of an extremely powerful autocomplete, trained on a huge fraction of all written text.
explanation.trap: Real-time internet search seems plausible because some assistants use it, but it is an add-on tool, not the way the model generates text.
explanation.rule: Understanding that an LLM generates probable, not verified, text is the basis for using it well in a bank: excellent for drafts and summaries, but numbers and sources must always be checked.

items.stem: In clinical drug development, which phase typically involves large trials with hundreds to thousands of patients, designed to confirm efficacy and safety before seeking regulatory approval?
options: Phase I
Phase II
Phase III
Phase IV

steps: Phase I: a small number of subjects, often healthy volunteers, to check safety and dosage. Phase II: tens or hundreds of patients, first evidence of efficacy and the optimal dose.

Phase III: large trials, often randomised and controlled, in hundreds or thousands of patients to confirm efficacy and safety; they form the basis of the application for approval to the FDA (US) or EMA (EU).
Phase IV: post-marketing studies, to monitor safety on a large scale.
explanation.shortcut: I = is it safe? II = does it work? III = does it really work at scale? IV = what happens in the real world?
explanation.trap: Phase IV can involve even more patients, but it takes place after approval, not before.
explanation.rule: A biotech's value jumps up or down on Phase II and III results: these are the binary events that healthcare analysts track.

items.stem: In the context of generative AI, a 'hallucination' is:
options: Fluent, confident output that is false or invented, such as a fake source
A model crashing because too many users query it at the same time
A model deliberately withholding from the user information that it holds
An image generated by a model from a written text prompt

steps: A hallucination is fluent, convincing but false output: invented data, non-existent citations, wrong numbers presented with confidence.
It arises because the model generates the most probable text, not verified text: if it does not know an answer it can still produce a plausible one.
It is reduced by connecting the model to verified sources (retrieval), asking for checkable citations and always keeping a human review.
explanation.shortcut: Hallucination = plausible but false.
explanation.trap: The idea that the model 'hides' information attributes intentions to software: the problem is unintentional invention, not omission.
explanation.rule: In a pitch book or a model a hallucinated number is a serious error: every figure produced with AI must be traced back to a primary source.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
options: To encrypt every email that a user sends and receives
To force users to change their password every month
To block every login attempt made from an unusual foreign country
To require two or more independent proofs of identity to log in

steps: MFA combines factors of different kinds: something you know (password), something you have (phone, token, security key) and something you are (fingerprint, face).
If an attacker steals the password, for example with a phishing email, they still cannot get in without the second factor.
Not all second factors are equal: SMS codes are weaker than authenticator apps or physical keys, which are more resistant to phishing.
explanation.shortcut: MFA = two different keys for the same door: if one is stolen, the door stays locked.
explanation.trap: Changing your password often seems prudent, but it does not protect against a password that has just been stolen; email encryption solves a different problem.
explanation.rule: Many incidents start from stolen credentials: MFA and vigilance against phishing are the first line of defence, and in finance regulators and clients take them for granted.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a ransomware attack?
options: Flooding a website with traffic to make it unavailable
Encrypting a victim's data and demanding payment to restore access
Tricking users into revealing passwords through fake emails
Secretly using a computer's processing power to mine cryptocurrency

steps: Ransomware is malware that encrypts the victim's data or locks its systems and demands a ransom, usually in cryptocurrency, in exchange for the decryption key.
'Double extortion' is now common: the data is also stolen and the attacker threatens to publish it if the ransom is not paid.
The main defences are isolated and tested backups, timely patching, MFA, network segmentation and incident response plans.
explanation.shortcut: Ransom = data held hostage in exchange for money.
explanation.trap: Flooding a website with traffic is a DDoS attack, which knocks the service offline but does not seize the data; scam emails are phishing, often the entry point for ransomware.
explanation.rule: Cyber risk is an operational and financial risk: an attack can halt production and hit revenue and reputation, and it is now a standard due diligence topic.

items.stem: A power plant's 'capacity factor' is:
options: Its maximum instantaneous output, measured in megawatts
The share of the energy contained in its fuel that is converted into electricity
Actual output over a period divided by the maximum possible at full capacity
The share of the electricity it generates that is lost in transmission

steps: Capacity factor = energy produced in the period / (rated capacity × hours in the period). A 100 MW plant that produces 219,000 MWh in a year has a factor of 25% (219,000 / 876,000).
Nuclear often exceeds 90%, offshore wind is around 40-50%, onshore wind around 25-35%, and solar PV typically between 10% and 25% depending on latitude.
This is why 1 GW of solar is not equivalent to 1 GW of nuclear: it produces far less energy in a year, and at different hours.
explanation.shortcut: Power (MW) is the most a plant can deliver, energy (MWh) is what it actually delivers: the capacity factor is the ratio between the two over time.
explanation.trap: The share of the fuel's energy converted into electricity is the plant's efficiency: confusing it with the capacity factor is the most common mistake.
explanation.rule: In renewable project finance models the capacity factor drives revenue: a few points of difference change the IRR and debt capacity.

items.stem: Roughly what share of drug candidates that enter Phase I clinical trials eventually receive regulatory approval?
options: About 10%
About 30%
About 50%
About 75%

steps: Industry studies estimate that only about one in ten drugs entering Phase I reaches approval, with large differences between therapeutic areas (oncology is among the hardest).
The main bottleneck is Phase II, where many molecules fail for lack of efficacy; even in Phase III a significant share does not make it through.
Developing a new drug typically takes 10-15 years from discovery to approval.
explanation.shortcut: Biotech = a portfolio of bets: about one in ten reaches the finish line.
explanation.trap: 50% seems reasonable if you think about one phase at a time, but the success probabilities of the individual phases multiply together.
explanation.rule: This is why biotechs are valued with an rNPV (risk-adjusted NPV): each cash flow is weighted by the probability of clearing the remaining phases.

items.stem: So-called 'green' hydrogen is produced by:
options: Steam methane reforming of natural gas, with carbon capture
Electrolysis of water powered by renewable electricity
Steam methane reforming of natural gas, without carbon capture
Gasification of coal or lignite, without carbon capture

steps: Green hydrogen: electrolysis of water (splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen) using renewable electricity, so with no direct CO2 emissions.

Grey hydrogen: from natural gas via steam methane reforming, emitting CO2; blue hydrogen: the same process but with CO2 capture and storage; coal gasification produces so-called black or brown hydrogen, the most polluting.
Today almost all the hydrogen produced in the world is fossil-based; green hydrogen still costs much more, mainly because of the cost of electricity and electrolysers.
explanation.shortcut: Green = water + renewable electricity; blue = gas + CO2 capture; grey = just gas.
explanation.trap: Blue hydrogen is often presented as clean, but it still starts from natural gas and is low-emission only if CO2 capture works well.
explanation.rule: The competitiveness of green hydrogen depends on the price of renewable electricity and on subsidies: a typical case where public policy determines whether projects are bankable.

items.stem: In the semiconductor industry, a 'fabless' company is one that:
options: Designs chips but outsources their manufacturing to foundries
Manufactures chips without the need for clean-room facilities
Makes only memory chips, rather than logic or processor chips
Sells the machines and tools that chip factories rely on

steps: A fabless company designs and sells chips but owns no factories (fabs): manufacturing is outsourced to a foundry.
The alternative model is the IDM (Integrated Device Manufacturer), which designs and manufactures in-house; a pure-play foundry manufactures chips designed by others.
The split arose because a leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars: concentrating production in a few foundries allows these costs to be shared across many customers.
explanation.shortcut: Fab-less = without a fab: design yes, manufacturing no.
explanation.trap: Companies that sell machinery for making chips belong to the equipment supply chain, a different segment with its own economics.
explanation.rule: The business model changes everything in valuation: a fabless company has high gross margins and little capex, a manufacturer has enormous capex and more pronounced cyclicality.

items.stem: In the economics of AI, 'inference' refers to:
options: Collecting and cleaning the data used to train a model
Running an already-trained model to answer users' requests
The initial training of a model on a large dataset
Human labelling of data to improve a model's accuracy

steps: Training is the phase in which the model learns from data: it requires enormous amounts of compute concentrated over a period, a largely upfront cost.
Inference is the use of the already trained model to respond to requests: every query consumes compute, so the cost grows with the number of users and the length of the responses.
As AI spreads, demand for inference compute is becoming an increasingly important component of spending on data centres and energy.
explanation.shortcut: Training = studying for the exam; inference = answering the questions, every time someone asks.
explanation.trap: Initial training is the best-known phase and the most expensive at any single moment, but it is not inference: confusing the two leads to underestimating recurring costs.
explanation.rule: To value an AI business, ask how much it costs to serve each user (inference cost) relative to what that user pays: that is the gross margin of the business model.

items.stem: In cybersecurity, a 'zero-day' vulnerability is:
options: An attack that lasts less than one day before it is stopped
A vulnerability fixed on the same day it is discovered
Malware programmed to activate at midnight on a set date
A flaw attackers can exploit before the vendor has a fix

steps: 'Zero-day' means the vendor has had zero days to fix the flaw: the vulnerability is unknown or has not yet been fixed with a patch.
Attacks exploiting zero-days are hard to prevent with traditional defences, and these vulnerabilities are highly valuable to attackers.
Once the patch is released the risk does not disappear: many organisations install it late and remain exposed to a vulnerability that is by then well known.
explanation.shortcut: Zero days' warning for those who have to defend themselves.
explanation.trap: A vulnerability fixed on the same day is the opposite of a zero-day: here the fix is missing altogether.
explanation.rule: Patch management and speed of response are indicators of cyber maturity that investors and regulators assess more and more often.

items.stem: The transformer architecture, on which most modern large language models are based, was introduced in a research paper published in which year?

steps: The transformer was presented in 2017 in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need', which introduced an 'attention' mechanism able to weigh, in parallel, the relationships between all the words in a text.
This parallelism made it possible to train much larger models using graphics processors, paving the way for LLMs.
2012 is the year of the deep learning breakthrough in image recognition; at the end of 2022 LLM-based chatbots reached the general public.
explanation.shortcut: 2012 deep learning for images, 2017 transformer, 2022 chatbots for everyone: about five years between each milestone.
explanation.trap: 2022 is the year many people associate with generative AI because that is when it took off with the public, but the underlying technology had existed for five years.
explanation.rule: Years often pass between invention and mass adoption: a good analyst distinguishes between the technological breakthrough and the moment it becomes a business.

items.stem: Today, a semiconductor process node name such as '5 nm' or '3 nm' is best described as:
options: The exact gate length of every transistor on the chip
The wavelength of the light used to print the circuits
A label for a technology generation, not a physical dimension
The thickness of the silicon wafer that the chips are cut from

steps: Until the '90s the node name roughly corresponded to the transistor gate length; then the two measures started to diverge, and with the three-dimensional transistors (FinFET) of the 2010s the link was lost altogether.

Today '3 nm' denotes a technology generation that is denser and higher-performing than the previous one, but no transistor dimension actually measures 3 nanometres, and different manufacturers use labels that are not comparable.
To compare technologies, industry practitioners look at metrics such as transistor density per square millimetre.
explanation.shortcut: The node's nanometre figure is like a model number: it tells you it is newer, not how big it is.
explanation.trap: The wavelength of the light used in lithography is something else: EUV lithography uses 13.5 nm light, yet it produces nodes called 5 or 3 nm.
explanation.rule: Faced with a technical or marketing label, an analyst always asks for the comparable underlying metric: this applies to chips as much as to 'adjusted' EBITDA.

items.stem: Why can the levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) understate the true cost of supplying power when solar and wind reach a high share of the grid?
options: It ignores capital costs and only counts operating costs
It double-counts the fuel costs of wind and solar plants
It is calculated in nominal terms, so it overstates the effect of inflation
It leaves out system costs such as backup, storage and grid upgrades

steps: LCOE is the average cost per MWh over the plant's life: the present value of costs (capex, opex, fuel) divided by the present value of the energy produced.

It measures the cost of the individual plant, not the cost of integrating it into the system: solar and wind produce when the sun shines or the wind blows, not when power is needed, and they require backup capacity, storage, grids and sometimes output cuts (curtailment).
Moreover, when many solar plants produce in the same hours, the market price in those hours collapses (cannibalisation effect), reducing the revenue actually captured.
explanation.shortcut: LCOE = the cost of producing a MWh, not the cost of delivering it when it is needed.
explanation.trap: LCOE does include capital costs, which for renewables are in fact the main component: that is precisely why it is very sensitive to the cost of capital.
explanation.rule: In renewable projects what matters is the capture price relative to LCOE, not LCOE on its own: it is the difference between a bankable project and one that is not.
